retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

The petitioner and her sister were arrested and initially detained under an Emergency Regulations detention order valid for ninety days, which expired on 12 November 1989. Despite expiration of legal authority, the petitioner remained in police custody for approximately one year without being produced before a Magistrate, and only later was remanded to fiscal custody. The State failed to justify continued detention or provide evidence supporting prolonged custody, raising issues under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning arbitrary arrest and detention and failure to produce a detainee before judicial authority within a reasonable time. The Supreme Court held that once the lawful detention order expired, any continued confinement without fresh valid authority was unconstitutional and amounted to unlawful detention. The Court emphasized that investigative convenience cannot override constitutional safeguards protecting personal liberty, and that prolonged detention without evidence of culpability is impermissible. It further noted that executive officers bear responsibility to ensure strict compliance with legal requirements governing deprivation of liberty. The Court declared the detention illegal, quashed relevant orders, and granted relief including compensation against the State and personal costs against the officer in charge. The decision reaffirmed strict judicial protection against arbitrary executive detention and reinforced the requirement of timely judicial oversight over custodial deprivation of liberty.

The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

The Petitioners, political and trade union leaders, were arrested following a bomb blast investigation and detained initially under time-bound orders, later converted into indefinite detention orders under Emergency Regulations. They alleged arbitrary arrest, illegal detention, and torture while in custody. The State justified detention based on suspected links to a suicide bomber. The Supreme Court held that arrests lacked credible supporting material and were not backed by contemporaneous records demonstrating reasonable suspicion. It further held that continued detention without disclosure of factual basis for executive satisfaction was arbitrary and contrary to constitutional safeguards. Although allegations of torture were raised, the Court found insufficient evidence to establish a violation of Article 11. It concluded that detention orders were unlawful and that Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were violated due to lack of objective justification and failure of evidentiary support. The Court ordered compensation and costs.

intake.harm_suffered: Alleged assault and threats at a police station, destruction of office premises by fire, loss of valuables and work materials, lack of proper police investigation, and disruption to professional work.
intake.user_narrative: I work as an Attorney-at-Law and have represented people who complained about unlawful arrest and torture by police officers. I went to the Negombo Police Station to obtain a copy of a complaint for a client-related matter. There was an argument about where I could park, and later I say a police officer threatened me and hit me. I complained about that incident. A few days later, my office beside my house in Ragama caught fire and was destroyed along with valuables and documents. I made a complaint to the Ragama Police, but I believe they failed to properly investigate what happened or try to find the people responsible.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court rejected the Article 11 complaint arising from the alleged police station assault because the conflicting versions and nature of the complaint did not satisfy the required threshold for torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court also rejected the Article 14(1)(g) claim because the petitioners did not substantiate that the failure to investigate prevented them from engaging in their professional duties. However, the Court held that the inaction of the Officer-in-Charge of Ragama Police Station in failing to properly investigate the complaint about the office being set on fire violated the petitioners' rights under Article 12(1), and the State was responsible for that inaction.
gold.gold_remedy: The State was directed to pay Rs. 50,000 as compensation to each petitioner within three months. No order was made as to costs.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name: De Silva v. Manoj and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was allegedly assaulted by a traffic police constable during a routine stop in Mount Lavinia after a brief exchange regarding vehicle documentation. The officer punched and kicked the petitioner without provocation, prompting a complaint and medical treatment. Although an internal inquiry resulted in a minor disciplinary warning, the petitioner filed a fundamental rights application alleging violation of Article 11. The respondent denied the assault, but evidence including medical records, prompt complaint, and inconsistent police documentation supported the petitioner's version. The Supreme Court found the denial not credible and held that corroborating evidence established the occurrence of physical violence. It concluded that law enforcement officers must act within constitutional limits and that unprovoked assault constitutes cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation against the officer personally as well as partial payment by the State. The decision emphasized accountability of police officers and the constitutional prohibition against unnecessary use of force.

cases.case_name: Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis, OIC Ginigathhena and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former employee of Brown and Company, was returning from an exorcism ritual performed for his son on February 28, 2007 when his vehicle encountered that of the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Ginigathhena Police Station, on a narrow road. Following a dispute over reversing the vehicles, the 1st Respondent assaulted the Petitioner and accused him of being a treasure hunter after observing ritual items inside the jeep. The Petitioner was arrested, transported to Kandy Police Station while bleeding and injured, and detained for approximately eighteen hours before being produced before a Magistrate, who observed that no offence appeared to have been committed. Medical evidence established grievous injuries including a fractured nasal bone and perforated ear drum caused by a blunt weapon. The Respondents attempted to justify the arrest by alleging treasure hunting activities and claimed the injuries were caused by a crowd. The Court rejected these explanations after the Archaeological Department confirmed that the location possessed no archaeological significance. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and that detention for eighteen hours without promptly recording a statement or producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate was arbitrary. The Court further ruled that the severe assault constituted cruel and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11. The Supreme Court found violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), ordered compensation against the 1st Respondent and the State, and condemned the use of barbarous police methods undermining public confidence.

cases.case_name: Sri Thaminda, Dharshane and Mahalekam v. Inspector of Police and Others
cases.summary: During a festival on August 11, 2003, the three Petitioners, who were intoxicated, became involved in a confrontation with police officers regarding the parking of a three-wheeler. A scuffle followed during which a Police Constable was injured and hospitalized. The Petitioners were arrested and later sustained multiple injuries. They alleged that police officers and members of the Rapid Deployment Force assaulted them while in custody, amounting to cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11. The Respondents contended that the injuries resulted from an angry crowd attempting to rescue the injured constable and denied responsibility for the assaults. The Supreme Court held that the arrests themselves were justified because the Petitioners had behaved aggressively and police intervention was necessary to prevent escalation of violence and maintain public order. Consequently, no violation of Article 13(1) was established. However, the Court found sufficient material to conclude that the Petitioners were assaulted by state officers acting under colour of office. The Court reaffirmed that constitutional protection against torture and cruel or degrading treatment applies irrespective of the victim's conduct. Nevertheless, the Court declined to award compensation because the Petitioners had themselves behaved in a disorderly and disgraceful manner and contributed to the circumstances leading to the incident. Declaratory relief alone was therefore granted for the infringement of Article 11.

retrieved_contexts: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The Petitioners, two Attorneys-at-Law, visited Ambalangoda Police Station on February 28, 2010, to represent a client whose relatives had allegedly been detained in connection with a child custody dispute following the death of the child's mother. The Petitioners alleged that the police had summoned the grieving family to the station and thereby prevented them from attending funeral arrangements. At the police station, the 1st and 2nd Respondents verbally abused the Petitioners, accused lawyers of earning money unfairly, threatened to arrest them for providing "wrong advice," and ordered them to switch off their mobile phones while coercing the family to surrender the child to the estranged father. The Petitioners contended that these acts violated Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court held that Article 11 protects against severe mental suffering intentionally inflicted by public officials and that humiliating and threatening legal practitioners in front of a bereaved family amounted to degrading treatment. The Court further held that lawyers possess a constitutional right to represent clients and that intimidation aimed at obstructing legal representation violated the freedom to engage in a lawful profession guaranteed by Article 14(1)(g). The Court rejected any justification for the conduct of the officers and observed that the Petitioners had acted professionally while the Respondents acted under colour of office in an arbitrary and abusive manner. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) and ordered the Respondents to personally pay compensation and litigation costs to the Petitioners.

The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

The petitioner was allegedly assaulted by a traffic police constable during a routine stop in Mount Lavinia after a brief exchange regarding vehicle documentation. The officer punched and kicked the petitioner without provocation, prompting a complaint and medical treatment. Although an internal inquiry resulted in a minor disciplinary warning, the petitioner filed a fundamental rights application alleging violation of Article 11. The respondent denied the assault, but evidence including medical records, prompt complaint, and inconsistent police documentation supported the petitioner's version. The Supreme Court found the denial not credible and held that corroborating evidence established the occurrence of physical violence. It concluded that law enforcement officers must act within constitutional limits and that unprovoked assault constitutes cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation against the officer personally as well as partial payment by the State. The decision emphasized accountability of police officers and the constitutional prohibition against unnecessary use of force.

intake.what_happened: We are Chief Inspectors of Police who were in the same batch and promoted to Chief Inspector along with another officer. Later, based on a political victimization relief process, that officer's promotion was backdated several years, placing him above us in seniority and making him eligible for consideration for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police ahead of us.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of equal treatment in police promotions, prejudice to seniority, reduced promotional prospects, and unfair disadvantage in consideration for the rank of Assistant Superintendent of Police.
intake.user_narrative: We are Chief Inspectors of Police who joined the police service around the same time as another officer and were promoted to Chief Inspector on the same date. Later, government and police authorities treated that officer as if he had been promoted to Chief Inspector several years earlier, based on a political victimization relief recommendation. This moved him above us in seniority and allowed him to be considered for the next promotion before us. We believe this unfairly affected our career progression and our chance to be considered equally for promotion.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the backdating of the 48th respondent's promotion to Chief Inspector of Police from 08 February 2020 to 01 January 2014 based on a political victimization relief process. The Court held that the Cabinet decision was not a valid policy decision applicable generally, but an ad hoc decision benefiting an individual, and that the backdating unfairly altered seniority and prejudiced the petitioners' promotional prospects. The Court found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) had been infringed, nullified the directives marked X13, X16 and X17, declared the backdating of the 48th respondent's appointment to Chief Inspector effective from 01 January 2014 illegal and of no force or effect, and declared that the 48th respondent was ineligible at the relevant time to be appointed Assistant Superintendent of Police.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear public-sector promotion and seniority violation case involving state actors and unlawful individual relief through a political victimization process. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 12(1): The facts suggest a potential violation of Article 12(1) as the backdating of another officer's promotion, based on a political victimization relief process, appears to have arbitrarily altered the petitioners' seniority and eligibility for promotion. This action by government and police promotion authorities may constitute unequal treatment before the law and a denial of equal protection, as it directly affected their career progression and consideration for promotion. Precedent cases (Dola Mullage Gunarathna, M.P.A.C. Pieris, Jayasundara) support that arbitrary changes to seniority lists and unfair promotion practices in public service can violate Article 12(1).
- Article 14(1)(g): The alleged act of backdating another officer's promotion, which resulted in the petitioners being placed below him in seniority and becoming ineligible for promotion consideration ahead of him, appears to directly impact their ability to engage in their lawful occupation (police service) and progress within it. This action, by affecting their promotional prospects and career progression, suggests an infringement on their right to engage in a lawful occupation. The Dola Mullage Gunarathna case (343) found a violation of Article 14(1)(g) in a similar context where retrospective backdating of promotions disrupted seniority and affected promotional prospects of police officers.

SECTION 2 — PRECEDENT:

cases.case_name: Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. It further held that seniority in public service constitutes a significant factor that cannot be disregarded absent clear evidence of unsuitability or exceptional merit in junior candidates. The failure of the Selection Board to explain the petitioner's exclusion rendered the process arbitrary and discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed. Accordingly, it directed the authorities to promote the petitioner with retrospective effect and awarded compensation.

retrieved_contexts: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

intake.user_narrative: We are Chief Inspectors of Police. We joined the police service on the same date as another officer, were promoted to Inspector on the same date, and became eligible for promotion to Chief Inspector on the same date. Later, a committee dealing with alleged political victimization recommended that this other officer's promotion be treated as if it had taken effect several years earlier. The Cabinet, Public Service Commission, Ministry of Public Security and Inspector-General of Police acted on that recommendation. This made him about six years senior to us and allowed him to be considered for promotion ahead of us. We believe this is unfair because he was in the same position as us and there was no proper basis to treat him differently.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the executive action backdating the 48th respondent's promotion to Chief Inspector of Police to 01 January 2014. The Court found that the petitioners and the 48th respondent were similarly circumstanced, having joined the police service on the same date, been promoted to Inspector on the same date, and become eligible for promotion to Chief Inspector on the same date. The sole basis for the political victimization recommendation was that the 48th respondent had served at Kalkuda Police Station, which the Court held could not justify treating him as politically victimized or backdating his promotion. The executive action therefore infringed the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were infringed, quashed the Political Victimization Committee recommendation to backdate the 48th respondent's promotion to 01 January 2014, quashed the Cabinet approval, quashed the Public Service Commission decision to implement it, and quashed its implementation by the Inspector-General of Police. The judgment was also directed to apply to SC FR 159/2022.

cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Gunawardana v. National Police Commission
cases.summary: The petitioners, Police Inspectors, challenged the cancellation of a completed recruitment process for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police, despite having successfully passed examinations and being placed on a merit list. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police cancelled the process based on a Cabinet decision to restructure the police service. The petitioners alleged violations of Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g), claiming deprivation of earned promotional rights. The Supreme Court held that once a competitive recruitment process is completed and a merit list is finalized, candidates acquire a legitimate expectation of promotion. It found that the retrospective cancellation of a valid selection process was arbitrary and irrational. The Court further held that while restructuring of public services is permissible, it cannot be used to nullify completed lawful processes without justification. It emphasized that administrative discretion must be exercised consistently with the rule of law and fairness. Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and quashed the impugned cancellation decisions.

cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

retrieved_contexts: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

intake.what_happened: I applied for internal promotion to the post of Technical Administrator at Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation. After interviews, a waiting list showed that I had higher marks than some employees who were later promoted to that post, but I was not promoted while they were appointed.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of fair consideration for internal promotion, adverse impact on career progression, and unequal treatment compared with lower-ranked candidates.
intake.user_narrative: I am an employee of Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation. I applied for internal promotion to the post of Technical Administrator. According to the waiting list, I had obtained higher interview marks than some employees who were later promoted. Even though I was placed above them on the list, they were appointed and I was left out. I believe this was unfair and affected my career progression within the corporation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) arising from appointments to the post of Technical Administrator. The Court held that it was unjustifiable to promote the 16th, 17th and 18th respondents over the 1st petitioner because the 1st petitioner had obtained higher marks on the waiting list. However, the 2nd and 3rd petitioners had the same marks as those respondents but were ranked lower and the promoted respondents were far senior in service. The Court declared only the 1st petitioner's Article 12(1) right violated and gave no final declaration under Article 14(1)(g).
gold.gold_remedy: The Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation and its Chairman were directed to appoint the 1st petitioner U.P.E. Wijesuriya to the post of Technical Administrator with effect from 01.08.2014, without arrears of salary, in the same manner as was done for the 15th to 18th respondents.

cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

cases.case_name: Weerasuriya Arachchige Leela Weerasuriya v. People's Bank and Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 419/2015, the petitioner, a senior officer at People's Bank, alleged that she was unfairly denied promotion to Deputy Head of Finance despite being qualified and repeatedly applying between 2009 and 2013. She contended that the Bank deliberately delayed recruitment processes, cancelled interviews without justification, and ultimately promoted a junior officer after ensuring he became eligible. The Supreme Court considered whether this conduct violated Article 12(1). It found that the repeated postponement and cancellation of recruitment processes lacked valid justification and demonstrated arbitrariness and lack of transparency. The Bank's explanation of restructuring was rejected as a pretext. The Court held that failure to disclose criteria or marks and the manipulation of timing in recruitment undermined fair competition. It emphasized that when a public institution undertakes selection for promotion, it must act reasonably, transparently, and consistently with equal treatment principles. The Court concluded that the petitioner's legitimate promotional expectations were frustrated through discriminatory administrative conduct. Accordingly, it held that her fundamental rights were violated and declared the actions of the Bank and officials unconstitutional under Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

stage_b_cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Weerasuriya Arachchige Leela Weerasuriya v. People's Bank and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 419/2015, the petitioner, a senior officer at People's Bank, alleged that she was unfairly denied promotion to Deputy Head of Finance despite being qualified and repeatedly applying between 2009 and 2013. She contended that the Bank deliberately delayed recruitment processes, cancelled interviews without justification, and ultimately promoted a junior officer after ensuring he became eligible. The Supreme Court considered whether this conduct violated Article 12(1). It found that the repeated postponement and cancellation of recruitment processes lacked valid justification and demonstrated arbitrariness and lack of transparency. The Bank's explanation of restructuring was rejected as a pretext. The Court held that failure to disclose criteria or marks and the manipulation of timing in recruitment undermined fair competition. It emphasized that when a public institution undertakes selection for promotion, it must act reasonably, transparently, and consistently with equal treatment principles. The Court concluded that the petitioner's legitimate promotional expectations were frustrated through discriminatory administrative conduct. Accordingly, it held that her fundamental rights were violated and declared the actions of the Bank and officials unconstitutional under Article 12(1).

stage_b_cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.
