retrieved_contexts: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

In SC(FR) Application No. 419/2015, the petitioner, a senior officer at People's Bank, alleged that she was unfairly denied promotion to Deputy Head of Finance despite being qualified and repeatedly applying between 2009 and 2013. She contended that the Bank deliberately delayed recruitment processes, cancelled interviews without justification, and ultimately promoted a junior officer after ensuring he became eligible. The Supreme Court considered whether this conduct violated Article 12(1). It found that the repeated postponement and cancellation of recruitment processes lacked valid justification and demonstrated arbitrariness and lack of transparency. The Bank's explanation of restructuring was rejected as a pretext. The Court held that failure to disclose criteria or marks and the manipulation of timing in recruitment undermined fair competition. It emphasized that when a public institution undertakes selection for promotion, it must act reasonably, transparently, and consistently with equal treatment principles. The Court concluded that the petitioner's legitimate promotional expectations were frustrated through discriminatory administrative conduct. Accordingly, it held that her fundamental rights were violated and declared the actions of the Bank and officials unconstitutional under Article 12(1).

The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

After a public administration salary circular, our salaries and pensions were enhanced through three salary increments and we received those payments for several years. Later, officials said the payments were erroneous, reduced our salaries and pensions, and moved to recover alleged overpayments from us.
intake.harm_suffered: Reduction of salary and pension benefits, threatened recovery of past payments, financial loss, uncertainty over retirement income, and unfair treatment after relying on payments made for several years.
intake.user_narrative: I work, or previously worked, in the Sri Lanka Technical Education Service. After a government salary circular, my salary or pension was increased with three increments, and this continued for several years. Later, the authorities suddenly said the increments had been given by mistake and decided to reduce my salary or pension and recover the amounts already paid. I had relied on those payments, especially for retirement and family expenses, and I believe it is unfair for the authorities to change their position after many years and recover money from us when the issue arose from their own circulars and decisions.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the reduction of salaries and pensions and the recovery of alleged overpayments after they had received three increments for several years under PA Circular 06/2006(VII). The Court held that the relevant circulars lacked clarity, that the respondents failed to justify the legal basis for recovering amounts paid from 2008 to 2012, and that the delay and arbitrary withdrawal of the increments violated the petitioners' right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were infringed, declared the decisions to recover the increments null and void, directed that those decisions be cancelled forthwith, refrained from awarding compensation because interim relief had restrained deductions, allowed both applications, and ordered parties to bear their own costs.

**Article 12(1) — Right to equality before the law**

1.  **Subject matter:** This article states that all persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
2.  **Explanation of applicability:** This article appears to apply because the facts describe a situation where public authorities, after issuing a salary circular that led to enhanced salaries and pensions for several years, later declared these payments erroneous and moved to reduce benefits and recover past payments. The officers had relied on these payments, and the issue appears to have arisen from the authorities' own circulars and decisions. The sudden reversal of a long-standing payment policy and the recovery of funds due to an administrative error originating with the authorities, after years of reliance, may suggest an arbitrary or unfair exercise of state power. Such arbitrary action by a public authority could be argued to be a denial of the equal protection of the law, as the state is expected to act fairly and consistently in its dealings with citizens.
3.  **Correspondence of facts to elements:**
    *   "All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law": The officers, as citizens, appear to be asserting a right to fair and consistent treatment by the state.
    *   "What happened: ...officials said the payments were erroneous, reduced our salaries and pensions, and moved to recover alleged overpayments from us." This action by the authorities, particularly after the payments were made for "several years" based on "their own circulars and decisions," suggests a potential for arbitrary state action.
    *   "Harm suffered: ...unfair treatment after relying on payments made for several years." This directly corresponds to the concept of a denial of equal protection if the state's actions are deemed arbitrary or inconsistent with principles of fairness and legitimate expectation.

cases.case_name:
F. A. Azeez v. H. M. Gunasekera, Secretary, Ministry of Education & Higher
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, appointed in 1999 to the Sri Lanka Education Administrative Service Class III, challenged the 2009 cancellation of her appointment and the State's attempt to recover approximately Rs. 1.9 million as alleged overpaid salary. The Respondents relied on a prior Supreme Court judgment invalidating the recruitment batch due to non-compliance with the national ethnic ratio requirement, asserting that the appointment was void ab initio. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging arbitrary deprivation of employment benefits after years of service. The Supreme Court held that the cancellation was not arbitrary but a necessary consequence of compliance with a binding judicial determination affecting the entire recruitment scheme. However, it found that the Petitioner had acted in good faith and performed duties for a decade without knowledge of illegality. The Court accepted that although the matter arose long prior, filing before the Human Rights Commission activated statutory protection under Section 13(1) regarding limitation. While upholding the cancellation, the Court exercised equitable jurisdiction to prevent recovery of salaries already paid, considering it unjust to penalise the Petitioner for administrative error not attributable to her. Accordingly, the application was dismissed with partial relief.

cases.case_name:
Padma Maithrilatha Akarawita and Others v. Dr. Nanda Wickramasinghe and
Others (Supra Grade Librarians Case)
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner, appointed in 1999 to the Sri Lanka Education Administrative Service Class III, challenged the 2009 cancellation of her appointment and the State's attempt to recover approximately Rs. 1.9 million as alleged overpaid salary. The Respondents relied on a prior Supreme Court judgment invalidating the recruitment batch due to non-compliance with the national ethnic ratio requirement, asserting that the appointment was void ab initio. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging arbitrary deprivation of employment benefits after years of service. The Supreme Court held that the cancellation was not arbitrary but a necessary consequence of compliance with a binding judicial determination affecting the entire recruitment scheme. However, it found that the Petitioner had acted in good faith and performed duties for a decade without knowledge of illegality. stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. Administration
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Freedom of association. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of association.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

The Petitioner, appointed in 1999 to the Sri Lanka Education Administrative Service Class III, challenged the 2009 cancellation of her appointment and the State's attempt to recover approximately Rs. 1.9 million as alleged overpaid salary. The Respondents relied on a prior Supreme Court judgment invalidating the recruitment batch due to non-compliance with the national ethnic ratio requirement, asserting that the appointment was void ab initio. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging arbitrary deprivation of employment benefits after years of service. The Supreme Court held that the cancellation was not arbitrary but a necessary consequence of compliance with a binding judicial determination affecting the entire recruitment scheme. However, it found that the Petitioner had acted in good faith and performed duties for a decade without knowledge of illegality. The Court accepted that although the matter arose long prior, filing before the Human Rights Commission activated statutory protection under Section 13(1) regarding limitation. While upholding the cancellation, the Court exercised equitable jurisdiction to prevent recovery of salaries already paid, considering it unjust to penalise the Petitioner for administrative error not attributable to her. Accordingly, the application was dismissed with partial relief.

The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

intake.what_happened: I was a Grade 11 student at a public school. My class teacher suspected me of being involved in a petition against her and often harassed me. One day before a term test, another teacher took me to her, and instead of only advising me about my haircut, she became angry and hit me hard on the head. I was sent to sit for the exam but left because of the pain. My father took me to hospital, where I was treated for an injury to my ear. When we complained to the principal, he did not conduct a proper and independent inquiry.
intake.harm_suffered: Physical assault at school, perforated left ear drum, temporary impairment of hearing, hospital treatment, pain, distress, and denial of a proper school-level inquiry.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Grade 11 student at a public school in Kurunegala. My English teacher had been treating me badly because she suspected that I had complained about her. On the day of a term test, another teacher stopped me and took me to her about my haircut. She became angry and hit me hard on the side of my head. I tried to sit for the exam but I was in too much pain and went home. My father took me to hospital, and doctors found that my ear drum had been injured. We complained to the principal, but he did not properly investigate what happened and seemed to protect the teacher.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the 1st respondent, a teacher at a public school acting under colour of office, assaulted the 1st petitioner student and caused a traumatic perforation of the left ear drum with temporary impairment of hearing. The Court found that the assault amounted to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment and infringed Article 11. The Court also held that the 2nd respondent principal failed to conduct an impartial and comprehensive inquiry and acted to shield the teacher, thereby depriving the petitioners of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The application was allowed. The Court declared that the 1st respondent infringed the 1st petitioner's Article 11 right and that the 2nd respondent infringed the 1st and 2nd petitioners' Article 12(1) rights. No heavy compensation was imposed because the 1st respondent had been in remand custody for seven months and had complied with a Court of Appeal compensation order. The petitioners were entitled to recover costs from the 1st respondent. The Secretary to the Ministry of Education was directed to issue a circular within nine months stating zero tolerance for physical or psychological harm to children as punishment, with the Attorney General to advise, and copies of the judgment were to be sent to the Attorney General and the Secretary to the Ministry of Education.

cases.case_name: Bandara v Wickremasinghe
cases.summary: The petitioner, a minor studying at Sri Subhuthi Vidyalaya, was summoned to the principal's office where he was assaulted by the Principal, Deputy Principal, Vice Principal, and a teacher. The assault included slapping and repeated blows with a cane, causing injuries to the petitioner's ear and face. The respondents claimed that the incident either constituted lawful disciplinary action or was a private act arising from tensions created by the petitioner's father regarding matters connected to a school sports meet. The petitioner alleged that the conduct violated Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and awarded compensation and costs against both the State and the individual respondents. The Court rejected the argument that the assault was a private act and held that the respondents, being public officers acting during school hours within the school environment, were engaged in executive or administrative action. Although school authorities possess disciplinary powers, the Court held that savage corporal punishment causing physical injury exceeded the limits of reasonable chastisement and amounted to unconstitutional treatment prohibited by Article 11. The Court relied on medical evidence confirming injuries consistent with the allegations and emphasized the personal responsibility of educators to avoid abuse of authority while exercising disciplinary functions within public educational institutions.

cases.case_name:
Mahapitiya Gedera Shanuka Gihan Karunaratne and Another v. Lory Koswatte
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, two schoolchildren, alleged that they were subjected to severe corporal punishment by the Deputy Principal after being wrongly accused of damaging school property. They were caned repeatedly, resulting in physical injuries and psychological trauma confirmed by medical evidence. They invoked Article 11 and Article 12(1), alleging cruel treatment and unequal protection of the law. The Supreme Court held that the conduct amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of constitutional guarantees. It further found that the Respondent acted in breach of Ministry of Education circulars prohibiting corporal punishment, and that such unlawful exercise of authority constituted arbitrary treatment under Article 12(1). The Court rejected the justification of disciplinary necessity, holding that teachers act under colour of office and remain subject to constitutional constraints. It also held that the State bears vicarious liability where there is a sufficient nexus between official duties and abusive conduct. Emphasising the heightened protection owed to children under domestic and international standards including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Court declared that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name: Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others alleged that following objections raised by the first petitioner regarding a school administrative appointment, his two children were subjected to harassment and assault by a teacher and school staff, and that the school authorities failed to take adequate action. They contended that this inaction forced the children to leave the school and constituted a violation of Article 12(1). The respondents demonstrated that prompt disciplinary measures were taken, including removal of the teacher from classroom duties, initiation of formal disciplinary proceedings, salary increment delays, and punitive transfer following findings of misconduct. An alternative school placement was also offered by education authorities. The Supreme Court examined whether there was arbitrary state inaction or discriminatory failure to protect the petitioners. It held that the authorities had acted with due diligence and that multiple corrective measures were taken in response to complaints. The Court further found that the alternative school offered was of comparable status and that the petitioners' refusal to accept it undermined the allegation of denial of educational access. It concluded that allegations of assault were not substantiated by independent evidence such as medical or police records. Accordingly, the Court held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Wijayasiriwardene v. Kumara, Inspector of Police, Kandy and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a sixteen-year-old student, was involved in a student demonstration during a period of civil unrest and was apprehended by police while attempting to join the gathering. He alleged that he was assaulted, resulting in injuries, including a slit lip and cheek injury. The respondent officer admitted to using a single blow but justified it as necessary to effect arrest in a volatile situation. The case involved Article 11 concerning freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Supreme Court assessed whether the use of force met the constitutional threshold of severity required to constitute Article 11 violation. It held that while police use of force must be reasonable and proportionate, not all instances of physical force amount to constitutional torture or degrading treatment. It found that the circumstances justified limited force in a chaotic environment and that there was no evidence of intentional humiliation or brutality. The Court concluded that although the force might have been excessive in a technical sense, it did not reach the constitutional standard of inhuman or degrading treatment. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation was found.

cases.case_name: Kankanige v. Senadheera and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner visited the BMICH on March 1, 2014, to purchase books and while searching for his motorbike in the parking area was confronted by police officers identified as the first to third respondents. Despite identifying himself as a medical student and producing identification documents, the officers verbally abused him, accused him of theft, and physically assaulted him. He was slapped, kicked, dragged by his hair, and suffered injuries including a perforated eardrum together with psychological trauma. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered personal compensation against each officer. The Court reasoned that Article 11 protects individuals not only from physical injury but also from psychological suffering and degrading treatment. Public humiliation, abusive language, and unjustified violence against a cooperative citizen constituted degrading and inhuman treatment prohibited by the Constitution. The Court further held that the medical evidence provided by the Judicial Medical Officer strongly corroborated the petitioner's account and rendered the respondents' explanation that the injuries resulted from a fall implausible. Emphasizing that police officers are required to exercise restraint and lawful authority, the Court concluded that the assault represented an arbitrary abuse of power incompatible with equal protection of the law and constitutional guarantees against cruel treatment.

retrieved_contexts: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

The petitioner, a minor studying at Sri Subhuthi Vidyalaya, was summoned to the principal's office where he was assaulted by the Principal, Deputy Principal, Vice Principal, and a teacher. The assault included slapping and repeated blows with a cane, causing injuries to the petitioner's ear and face. The respondents claimed that the incident either constituted lawful disciplinary action or was a private act arising from tensions created by the petitioner's father regarding matters connected to a school sports meet. The petitioner alleged that the conduct violated Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and awarded compensation and costs against both the State and the individual respondents. The Court rejected the argument that the assault was a private act and held that the respondents, being public officers acting during school hours within the school environment, were engaged in executive or administrative action. Although school authorities possess disciplinary powers, the Court held that savage corporal punishment causing physical injury exceeded the limits of reasonable chastisement and amounted to unconstitutional treatment prohibited by Article 11. The Court relied on medical evidence confirming injuries consistent with the allegations and emphasized the personal responsibility of educators to avoid abuse of authority while exercising disciplinary functions within public educational institutions.

The Petitioners, two schoolchildren, alleged that they were subjected to severe corporal punishment by the Deputy Principal after being wrongly accused of damaging school property. They were caned repeatedly, resulting in physical injuries and psychological trauma confirmed by medical evidence. They invoked Article 11 and Article 12(1), alleging cruel treatment and unequal protection of the law. The Supreme Court held that the conduct amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of constitutional guarantees. It further found that the Respondent acted in breach of Ministry of Education circulars prohibiting corporal punishment, and that such unlawful exercise of authority constituted arbitrary treatment under Article 12(1). The Court rejected the justification of disciplinary necessity, holding that teachers act under colour of office and remain subject to constitutional constraints. It also held that the State bears vicarious liability where there is a sufficient nexus between official duties and abusive conduct. Emphasising the heightened protection owed to children under domestic and international standards including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Court declared that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered compensation.

The petitioners in Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others alleged that following objections raised by the first petitioner regarding a school administrative appointment, his two children were subjected to harassment and assault by a teacher and school staff, and that the school authorities failed to take adequate action. They contended that this inaction forced the children to leave the school and constituted a violation of Article 12(1). The respondents demonstrated that prompt disciplinary measures were taken, including removal of the teacher from classroom duties, initiation of formal disciplinary proceedings, salary increment delays, and punitive transfer following findings of misconduct. An alternative school placement was also offered by education authorities. The Supreme Court examined whether there was arbitrary state inaction or discriminatory failure to protect the petitioners. It held that the authorities had acted with due diligence and that multiple corrective measures were taken in response to complaints. The Court further found that the alternative school offered was of comparable status and that the petitioners' refusal to accept it undermined the allegation of denial of educational access. It concluded that allegations of assault were not substantiated by independent evidence such as medical or police records. Accordingly, the Court held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Dasanayakage Gayani Geethika and Others v. D.M.D. Dissanayake, Principal,
D.S. Senanayake College and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners sought admission of the 3rd Petitioner to Grade 1 at D.S. Senanayake College for the year 2011 under the category applicable to residents living in close proximity to the school. The school selection panel awarded zero marks for residence, concluding that the Petitioners had failed to prove occupation of the stated address because the lease agreement was unregistered and because they did not possess formal title documents such as deeds or gift transfers. The Petitioners produced several documents in support of their claim, including a lease agreement, electoral register extracts, utility bills, and bank statements consistently reflecting the same address over a substantial period. The Petitioners alleged that the rejection violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court held that the selection panel had acted arbitrarily by focusing narrowly on the absence of stereotyped ownership documents while disregarding the cumulative evidentiary value of the materials produced. It emphasized that residence must be assessed in a practical and realistic manner rather than according to rigid notions of title documentation. The Court found that the totality of the evidence, including utility records and electoral documentation, sufficiently established genuine residence at the relevant address. Although acknowledging the administrative burden on school selection panels, the Court held that authorities were nevertheless required to act reasonably and fairly in evaluating applications. The Supreme Court concluded that the rejection based upon a fixed and unreasonable approach to documentary proof violated the Petitioners' right to equality and equal protection of the law and directed the immediate admission of the 3rd Petitioner to the school.

cases.case_name:
Nanayakkara and Others v. S.S.K. Aviruppola, Principal, Visakha Vidyalaya and
Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 24/2018, parents challenged the rejection of their child's admission to Grade 1 at Visakha Vidyalaya under the proximity category. The School Selection Committee awarded reduced marks for residence, disputing the authenticity and continuity of claimed residence despite lease agreements and utility documentation. The respondents alleged that the address was temporary or falsely declared to gain admission advantage. The Supreme Court considered whether the assessment violated Article 12(1). It held that while schools have discretion in evaluating admissions, such discretion must be exercised fairly, transparently, and in accordance with published criteria. The Court found that the rejection of documentary evidence without objective reasoning and reliance on a superficial field inquiry rendered the decision arbitrary. It emphasized that administrative decisions affecting education must be consistent and non-discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioners had sufficiently demonstrated residence under the applicable guidelines and that denial of marks lacked rational justification. Accordingly, it held that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and ordered admission of the child subject to verification of documents.

cases.case_name:
S.M.N.S. Thilakarathne and Another v. M.W.D.T.P. Wanasinghe, Principal,
Dharmaraja College and Others
cases.summary: The 1st Petitioner applied for Grade 1 admission for her son to Dharmaraja College, Kandy, under the close proximity category provided in Circular No. 22/2017. The application was rejected because the Petitioners failed to achieve the minimum qualifying score of 85 marks, having obtained only 76.25 marks. The Petitioners challenged the allocation of residency marks, asserting that the ownership period of the Petitioner's father should have been aggregated with her own period of ownership for purposes of calculating marks. They also disputed deductions made on the basis that several other schools were geographically closer to their residence than Dharmaraja College. Invoking Article 12(1), the Petitioners alleged arbitrary and discriminatory treatment in the admissions process. The Court dismissed the application and held that the Respondents had correctly applied the provisions of Circular No. 22/2017. It reasoned that the Circular expressly calculated residency marks according to the duration of ownership held by the applicant or spouse, and therefore prior ownership by the Petitioner's father could not be considered. The Court further held that the Circular required the use of official aerial maps prepared by the Department of the Surveyor General to determine proximity, and those maps established that the schools identified by the Respondents were in fact nearer to the residence. The allegation of unequal treatment was rejected because no evidence of bias or arbitrary marking against similarly situated applicants in the same academic year was established.

cases.case_name: Pavithra Tharangi Illeperuma v. Principal, Visakha Vidyalaya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner sought admission of her daughter to Visakha Vidyalaya for Grade 1 under the "close proximity" category, challenging the School Appeal Board's refusal to award full residence-related marks. The initial rejection occurred on an erroneous assumption regarding the child's religion, later corrected on appeal, where the Board awarded 47 marks but denied full residential marks due to the family's movement between two adjoining apartment units within the same building during the relevant five-year period. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging unequal treatment and arbitrary evaluation of eligibility criteria. The Supreme Court held that the Appeal Board's approach was excessively literal and failed to adopt a purposive interpretation of residence requirements under the admission circulars. It found that continuous residence was substantively satisfied as the two units were functionally part of the same residential occupation, separated only by a wall and not constituting a meaningful change of residence. The Court further held that denial of marks for additional documentation lacked textual support in the governing circular and amounted to arbitrary deviation from established criteria. It also noted inconsistency in administrative practice, as another national school had accepted identical documentation for full marks under the same framework. The Court rejected arguments relating to natural barriers, finding no rational basis for differential treatment. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioner was entitled to sufficient marks exceeding the cut-off and ordered admission of the child.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

The Petitioners sought admission of the 3rd Petitioner to Grade 1 at D.S. Senanayake College for the year 2011 under the category applicable to residents living in close proximity to the school. The school selection panel awarded zero marks for residence, concluding that the Petitioners had failed to prove occupation of the stated address because the lease agreement was unregistered and because they did not possess formal title documents such as deeds or gift transfers. The Petitioners produced several documents in support of their claim, including a lease agreement, electoral register extracts, utility bills, and bank statements consistently reflecting the same address over a substantial period. The Petitioners alleged that the rejection violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court held that the selection panel had acted arbitrarily by focusing narrowly on the absence of stereotyped ownership documents while disregarding the cumulative evidentiary value of the materials produced. It emphasized that residence must be assessed in a practical and realistic manner rather than according to rigid notions of title documentation. The Court found that the totality of the evidence, including utility records and electoral documentation, sufficiently established genuine residence at the relevant address. Although acknowledging the administrative burden on school selection panels, the Court held that authorities were nevertheless required to act reasonably and fairly in evaluating applications. The Supreme Court concluded that the rejection based upon a fixed and unreasonable approach to documentary proof violated the Petitioners' right to equality and equal protection of the law and directed the immediate admission of the 3rd Petitioner to the school.

In SC(FR) Application No. 24/2018, parents challenged the rejection of their child's admission to Grade 1 at Visakha Vidyalaya under the proximity category. The School Selection Committee awarded reduced marks for residence, disputing the authenticity and continuity of claimed residence despite lease agreements and utility documentation. The respondents alleged that the address was temporary or falsely declared to gain admission advantage. The Supreme Court considered whether the assessment violated Article 12(1). It held that while schools have discretion in evaluating admissions, such discretion must be exercised fairly, transparently, and in accordance with published criteria. The Court found that the rejection of documentary evidence without objective reasoning and reliance on a superficial field inquiry rendered the decision arbitrary. It emphasized that administrative decisions affecting education must be consistent and non-discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioners had sufficiently demonstrated residence under the applicable guidelines and that denial of marks lacked rational justification. Accordingly, it held that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and ordered admission of the child subject to verification of documents.

The petitioners challenged the denial of school admission under a proximity-based quota system, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The authorities rejected admission to Grade 1 at a national school despite ownership of the residential premises and supporting utility documentation. The dispute centered on whether authorities could distinguish between two houses within the same family compound for proximity calculation purposes. The respondents argued that the application was based on incorrect residency representation and that the relevant assessment should be made from the actual occupied house used for residence. The Supreme Court held that where a family owns an entire property compound and no competing occupancy exists, school authorities cannot arbitrarily distinguish between buildings within the same premises for admission assessment. It found that the rejection was based on an unjustified investigative approach that treated internal residential arrangement as determinative. The Court emphasized that documentary evidence already supported the petitioners' residence claim and that authorities had no basis to override ownership and occupancy facts. It concluded that the denial of admission was arbitrary and amounted to unequal treatment under Article 12(1). The Court declared a violation and ordered immediate admission of the child.

intake.incident_location: Tangalle STF Camp and Tissamaharama Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Tissamaharama Police Station
intake.what_happened: I am a Police Constable attached to the Special Task Force. Police officers came to the STF camp and questioned me about an alleged theft of valuable Valampuri shells. I was later handed over to the Tissamaharama Police Station and kept there for several days before being produced before a Magistrate. I say there was no proper evidence against me and that I was kept in custody before the police formally recorded my arrest.
intake.harm_suffered: Arbitrary arrest, unlawful detention for several days before judicial production, remand custody, interdiction from service, reputational harm and financial hardship.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Police Constable attached to the Special Task Force. Police officers came to my camp and questioned me about an alleged theft of valuable Valampuri shells. The next day I was handed over to the Tissamaharama Police Station. I was kept there in custody for several days before being produced before a Magistrate, even though I believe there was no proper evidence against me. I was later remanded, not identified at an identification parade, and then released on bail. After that, I was interdicted from service because of the arrest and remand. This caused serious harm to my liberty, reputation and employment.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged unlawful arrest, unlawful detention and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment by police officers. The Court found that the police acted without sufficient objectively verifiable material to justify the arrest and that the petitioner had in fact been in police custody from 28 April 2012, although formal arrest was recorded only on 30 April 2012, and was not produced before a Magistrate within the required time. Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were therefore violated by the 1st, 2nd and 3rd respondents and the State. The Article 11 allegation was rejected because the petitioner failed to provide sufficient supporting evidence, medical material or independent corroboration of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.
gold.gold_remedy: The 1st, 2nd and 3rd respondents were each directed to pay Rs. 250,000 from their personal funds to the petitioner, and the State was directed to pay a further Rs. 50,000 as compensation.
gold.evaluation_notes: Partial-violation police arrest and detention case. Useful for testing overclaiming control because Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were accepted while the Article 11 torture or cruel-treatment claim was rejected for lack of proof. cases.case_name: Piyasiri and Others v. Nimal Fernando, A.S.P. and Others
cases.summary: Fourteen Customs Officers at Katunayake Airport were stopped, questioned, and taken to a police station by officers investigating alleged bribery. They were searched and money was found in their possession, but they were not informed of specific charges or reasons for arrest. The Petitioners challenged their detention under Article 13(1), alleging arbitrary arrest without disclosure of grounds. The State argued that the actions were part of an ongoing corruption investigation. The Supreme Court held that arrest based on vague or general suspicion does not satisfy constitutional requirements and must be supported by specific and credible information. It further held that arrest cannot be used as a mechanism to gather evidence through subsequent search procedures. The Court emphasized that even if individuals move under police direction, they remain in custody if their liberty is restrained. It found that the failure to communicate a precise reason for arrest constituted a breach of mandatory constitutional safeguards. The Court concluded that the Petitioners were subjected to arbitrary arrest in violation of Article 13(1) and awarded compensation.

cases.case_name: Kapugama v. Krishantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested at a roadblock while travelling from Jaffna to Kandy after police discovered a large sum of cash in his possession, which he explained was intended for a land transaction and supported with documentation. Despite this explanation, he was detained at Vavuniya Police Station, and a B-report later falsely stated that he refused to provide a statement. The petitioner alleged violations of Article 13(1) relating to freedom from arbitrary arrest. The respondents failed to establish reasonable suspicion of any cognizable offence, relying solely on possession of cash without considering the petitioner's explanation and supporting documents. The Supreme Court found that mere possession of money, in the absence of incriminating material, did not justify arrest under criminal procedure law. The Court further held that the B-report was misleading and contradicted by evidence, demonstrating procedural irregularity and lack of lawful basis for producing the petitioner before a Magistrate. It concluded that the arrest was not carried out in accordance with procedure established by law and therefore constituted arbitrary deprivation of liberty. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation against the responsible police officers for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name: Namasivayam v. Gunawardena
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested by a police officer at Nawalapitiya on suspicion of involvement in a robbery investigation and taken into custody without being informed of the reason for arrest at the time. He was later taken to a security camp and police station, where he alleged assault and coercion to make a statement. cases.case_name:
Hettiarachchige Srimathi Devika Tissera and Others v. Police Constable
Jayasekara and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Hettiarachchige Srimathi Devika Tissera and Others v. Police Constable Jayasekara and Others arose from an incident on Christmas Eve 2012 in Ja-Ela where a family dispute over a parked vehicle escalated into police intervention. The petitioners alleged that police officers verbally abused them, forcibly removed the daughter from the vehicle, and assaulted the minor son. They were taken to the police station and detained for several hours without explanation, effectively amounting to an unlawful deprivation of liberty, and were later formally arrested and remanded on allegations of assaulting police officers. A Special Investigations Unit later found procedural irregularities, including false entries in official records and misconduct by the officer-in-charge. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1) and 13(1), alleging unequal treatment and arbitrary arrest. The Court held that keeping individuals confined at a police station without lawful justification constituted an implicit arrest, even in the absence of formal declaration. It further found that failure to inform the petitioners of reasons for arrest at the earliest opportunity violated mandatory procedural safeguards under Article 13(1). The Court also found the arrest to be arbitrary and supported by falsified documentation, rendering the State action unconstitutional. Accordingly, the Court held that Article 13(1) had been violated, affirmed the infringement of personal liberty, and awarded compensation against both the responsible officers and the State for unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.
