retrieved_contexts: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

Fourteen Customs Officers at Katunayake Airport were stopped, questioned, and taken to a police station by officers investigating alleged bribery. They were searched and money was found in their possession, but they were not informed of specific charges or reasons for arrest. The Petitioners challenged their detention under Article 13(1), alleging arbitrary arrest without disclosure of grounds. The State argued that the actions were part of an ongoing corruption investigation. The Supreme Court held that arrest based on vague or general suspicion does not satisfy constitutional requirements and must be supported by specific and credible information. It further held that arrest cannot be used as a mechanism to gather evidence through subsequent search procedures. The Court emphasized that even if individuals move under police direction, they remain in custody if their liberty is restrained. It found that the failure to communicate a precise reason for arrest constituted a breach of mandatory constitutional safeguards. The Court concluded that the Petitioners were subjected to arbitrary arrest in violation of Article 13(1) and awarded compensation.

The petitioner was arrested at a roadblock while travelling from Jaffna to Kandy after police discovered a large sum of cash in his possession, which he explained was intended for a land transaction and supported with documentation. Despite this explanation, he was detained at Vavuniya Police Station, and a B-report later falsely stated that he refused to provide a statement. The petitioner alleged violations of Article 13(1) relating to freedom from arbitrary arrest. The respondents failed to establish reasonable suspicion of any cognizable offence, relying solely on possession of cash without considering the petitioner's explanation and supporting documents. The Supreme Court found that mere possession of money, in the absence of incriminating material, did not justify arrest under criminal procedure law. The Court further held that the B-report was misleading and contradicted by evidence, demonstrating procedural irregularity and lack of lawful basis for producing the petitioner before a Magistrate. It concluded that the arrest was not carried out in accordance with procedure established by law and therefore constituted arbitrary deprivation of liberty. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation against the responsible police officers for the unlawful arrest and detention.

The Petitioner was arrested by a police officer at Nawalapitiya on suspicion of involvement in a robbery investigation and taken into custody without being informed of the reason for arrest at the time. He was later taken to a security camp and police station, where he alleged assault and coercion to make a statement. The Respondents justified the arrest on suspicion of the Petitioner being acquainted with facts relating to a gun robbery. The constitutional issue concerned Article 13(1), requiring that a person arrested must be informed of the reason for arrest at the time of arrest. The Supreme Court held that this requirement is a fundamental safeguard of personal liberty under the rule of law and imposes a mandatory duty on arresting officers. The Court emphasized that suspicion alone is insufficient unless it is contemporaneously communicated to the arrested person to enable understanding and challenge of the basis of detention. It found that the arresting officer admitted the arrest but failed to establish that the reason was communicated at the time of arrest. Although allegations under Articles 11 and 13(2) were raised, the Court found insufficient evidence to support them. The Court concluded that the failure to inform the Petitioner of the reason for arrest constituted a violation of Article 13(1), and awarded compensation against the State.

intake.user_narrative: I applied for my son's Grade One admission to Royal College because we had been living close to the school for many years under registered lease agreements. I submitted the lease documents, land registry extracts, electoral register extracts, a Grama Niladhari residence certificate and other documents to prove our residence. At the interview, the panel refused to give us marks because they said the lease did not meet the required validity period. Later, after an amendment to the circular, our appeal was rejected again based on a cut-off date that was introduced after the application process. I believe this unfairly denied my child admission even though we had continuously lived within the feeder area.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

ACT/OMISSION: Public school officials and education officials refused to award marks for Grade One admission and subsequently rejected an appeal.
CIRCUMSTANCES: The initial refusal to award marks was based on the assertion that the submitted lease agreements did not meet a required validity period, despite the user having lived within the feeder area for many years under successive registered lease agreements and submitting various documents to prove residence. The subsequent appeal was rejected based on a cut-off date that was introduced after the application process and after an amendment to the circular.
DIRECT CONSEQUENCES: The user's child was denied admission to Royal College.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

cases.case_name:
Nanayakkara and Others v. S.S.K. Aviruppola, Principal, Visakha Vidyalaya and
Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 24/2018, parents challenged the rejection of their child's admission to Grade 1 at Visakha Vidyalaya under the proximity category. The School Selection Committee awarded reduced marks for residence, disputing the authenticity and continuity of claimed residence despite lease agreements and utility documentation. The respondents alleged that the address was temporary or falsely declared to gain admission advantage. The Supreme Court considered whether the assessment violated Article 12(1). It held that while schools have discretion in evaluating admissions, such discretion must be exercised fairly, transparently, and in accordance with published criteria. The Court found that the rejection of documentary evidence without objective reasoning and reliance on a superficial field inquiry rendered the decision arbitrary. It emphasized that administrative decisions affecting education must be consistent and non-discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioners had sufficiently demonstrated residence under the applicable guidelines and that denial of marks lacked rational justification. Accordingly, it held that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and ordered admission of the child subject to verification of documents.

cases.case_name:
S.M.N.S. Thilakarathne and Another v. M.W.D.T.P. Wanasinghe, Principal,
Dharmaraja College and Others
cases.summary: The 1st Petitioner applied for Grade 1 admission for her son to Dharmaraja College, Kandy, under the close proximity category provided in Circular No. 22/2017. The application was rejected because the Petitioners failed to achieve the minimum qualifying score of 85 marks, having obtained only 76.25 marks. The Petitioners challenged the allocation of residency marks, asserting that the ownership period of the Petitioner's father should have been aggregated with her own period of ownership for purposes of calculating marks. They also disputed deductions made on the basis that several other schools were geographically closer to their residence than Dharmaraja College. Invoking Article 12(1), the Petitioners alleged arbitrary and discriminatory treatment in the admissions process. The Court dismissed the application and held that the Respondents had correctly applied the provisions of Circular No. 22/2017. It reasoned that the Circular expressly calculated residency marks according to the duration of ownership held by the applicant or spouse, and therefore prior ownership by the Petitioner's father could not be considered. The Court further held that the Circular required the use of official aerial maps prepared by the Department of the Surveyor General to determine proximity, and those maps established that the schools identified by the Respondents were in fact nearer to the residence. The allegation of unequal treatment was rejected because no evidence of bias or arbitrary marking against similarly situated applicants in the same academic year was established.

cases.case_name: Pavithra Tharangi Illeperuma v. Principal, Visakha Vidyalaya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner sought admission of her daughter to Visakha Vidyalaya for Grade 1 under the "close proximity" category, challenging the School Appeal Board's refusal to award full residence-related marks. The initial rejection occurred on an erroneous assumption regarding the child's religion, later corrected on appeal, where the Board awarded 47 marks but denied full residential marks due to the family's movement between two adjoining apartment units within the same building during the relevant five-year period. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging unequal treatment and arbitrary evaluation of eligibility criteria. The Supreme Court held that the Appeal Board's approach was excessively literal and failed to adopt a purposive interpretation of residence requirements under the admission circulars. It found that continuous residence was substantively satisfied as the two units were functionally part of the same residential occupation, separated only by a wall and not constituting a meaningful change of residence. The Court further held that denial of marks for additional documentation lacked textual support in the governing circular and amounted to arbitrary deviation from established criteria. It also noted inconsistency in administrative practice, as another national school had accepted identical documentation for full marks under the same framework. The Court rejected arguments relating to natural barriers, finding no rational basis for differential treatment. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioner was entitled to sufficient marks exceeding the cut-off and ordered admission of the child.

cases.case_name:
D. Wathsala Subhashini De Silva and Another v. Hasitha Kesara Wettimuni and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged the denial of school admission under a proximity-based quota system, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The authorities rejected admission to Grade 1 at a national school despite ownership of the residential premises and supporting utility documentation. The dispute centered on whether authorities could distinguish between two houses within the same family compound for proximity calculation purposes. The respondents argued that the application was based on incorrect residency representation and that the relevant assessment should be made from the actual occupied house used for residence. The Supreme Court held that where a family owns an entire property compound and no competing occupancy exists, school authorities cannot arbitrarily distinguish between buildings within the same premises for admission assessment. It found that the rejection was based on an unjustified investigative approach that treated internal residential arrangement as determinative. The Court emphasized that documentary evidence already supported the petitioners' residence claim and that authorities had no basis to override ownership and occupancy facts. It concluded that the denial of admission was arbitrary and amounted to unequal treatment under Article 12(1). The Court declared a violation and ordered immediate admission of the child.

cases.case_name:
Paalawa Rankoth Gedara Kenudi Dilandi and Another v. Sandamali Aviruppola,
Principal of Visakha Vidyalaya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners challenged the reduction of marks during the Grade 1 admission process to Visakha Vidyalaya, where a valid Urban Development Authority housing installment agreement was initially awarded full marks under the "close proximity" category but later reduced to a lower score, resulting in failure to meet the admission cut-off. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) on equality and equal protection. The Supreme Court held that the Respondents acted arbitrarily by disregarding mandatory criteria in the School Admission Circular, which expressly recognised installment housing agreements as qualifying documents for full marks. It found that the Petitioners had complied fully with documentary requirements and that the subsequent reclassification lacked rational justification. The Court further held that penalising applicants for benefiting from state housing schemes amounted to indirect economic discrimination and undermined equality in educational access. It emphasised that similarly placed applicants must be treated alike and that administrative deviation from published criteria constitutes unequal treatment. Accordingly, the Court concluded that the Petitioners were deprived of equal protection of the law and declared that their fundamental rights had been infringed, directing admission of the child to the school.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

In SC(FR) Application No. 24/2018, parents challenged the rejection of their child's admission to Grade 1 at Visakha Vidyalaya under the proximity category. The School Selection Committee awarded reduced marks for residence, disputing the authenticity and continuity of claimed residence despite lease agreements and utility documentation. The respondents alleged that the address was temporary or falsely declared to gain admission advantage. The Supreme Court considered whether the assessment violated Article 12(1). It held that while schools have discretion in evaluating admissions, such discretion must be exercised fairly, transparently, and in accordance with published criteria. The Court found that the rejection of documentary evidence without objective reasoning and reliance on a superficial field inquiry rendered the decision arbitrary. It emphasized that administrative decisions affecting education must be consistent and non-discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioners had sufficiently demonstrated residence under the applicable guidelines and that denial of marks lacked rational justification. Accordingly, it held that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and ordered admission of the child subject to verification of documents.

The 1st Petitioner applied for Grade 1 admission for her son to Dharmaraja College, Kandy, under the close proximity category provided in Circular No. 22/2017. The application was rejected because the Petitioners failed to achieve the minimum qualifying score of 85 marks, having obtained only 76.25 marks. The Petitioners challenged the allocation of residency marks, asserting that the ownership period of the Petitioner's father should have been aggregated with her own period of ownership for purposes of calculating marks. They also disputed deductions made on the basis that several other schools were geographically closer to their residence than Dharmaraja College. Invoking Article 12(1), the Petitioners alleged arbitrary and discriminatory treatment in the admissions process. The Court dismissed the application and held that the Respondents had correctly applied the provisions of Circular No. 22/2017. It reasoned that the Circular expressly calculated residency marks according to the duration of ownership held by the applicant or spouse, and therefore prior ownership by the Petitioner's father could not be considered. The Court further held that the Circular required the use of official aerial maps prepared by the Department of the Surveyor General to determine proximity, and those maps established that the schools identified by the Respondents were in fact nearer to the residence. The allegation of unequal treatment was rejected because no evidence of bias or arbitrary marking against similarly situated applicants in the same academic year was established.

The Petitioner sought admission of her daughter to Visakha Vidyalaya for Grade 1 under the "close proximity" category, challenging the School Appeal Board's refusal to award full residence-related marks. The initial rejection occurred on an erroneous assumption regarding the child's religion, later corrected on appeal, where the Board awarded 47 marks but denied full residential marks due to the family's movement between two adjoining apartment units within the same building during the relevant five-year period. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging unequal treatment and arbitrary evaluation of eligibility criteria. The Supreme Court held that the Appeal Board's approach was excessively literal and failed to adopt a purposive interpretation of residence requirements under the admission circulars. It found that continuous residence was substantively satisfied as the two units were functionally part of the same residential occupation, separated only by a wall and not constituting a meaningful change of residence. The Court further held that denial of marks for additional documentation lacked textual support in the governing circular and amounted to arbitrary deviation from established criteria. It also noted inconsistency in administrative practice, as another national school had accepted identical documentation for full marks under the same framework. The Court rejected arguments relating to natural barriers, finding no rational basis for differential treatment. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioner was entitled to sufficient marks exceeding the cut-off and ordered admission of the child.

cases.case_name: CH.A. Manoj Talis v. Inspector Hiriyadeniya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

It held that the arrest and detention of the second Petitioner were arbitrary due to the absence of lawful justification or communication of grounds. The Court emphasized that police officers must act strictly within legal authority and that custodial violence constitutes a serious breach of constitutional protections. It also imposed personal liability on the officers involved, reinforcing accountability for State agents. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and awarded compensation.

cases.case_name:
Erandaka and Another v. Halwela, Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Hakmana
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners were arrested on suspicion of theft of a water pump and examined medically at the time of arrest with no injuries recorded. They were remanded the same day. After eight days in custody, a Judicial Medical Officer found multiple contusions on both Petitioners. They alleged torture by police officers at the station and by prison guards while in State custody. The constitutional issue concerned Article 11 protection against torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The State argued lack of proof identifying specific perpetrators and inconsistent accounts. The Supreme Court held that the timing of injuries, emerging only after remand while absent at arrest, established a strong inference that the injuries were inflicted during State custody. It further held that the State bears strict responsibility for persons in its custody regardless of identification of individual offenders. The Court emphasized that executive or administrative action resulting in custodial harm violates constitutional guarantees. It found liability even without direct attribution to named officers, since custody implies a duty of care and protection. The Court concluded that Article 11 had been violated and awarded compensation against the State, affirming that custodial torture engages strict constitutional accountability.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

The Petitioner was arrested following a land dispute and alleged that while in police custody he was subjected to severe assault resulting in permanent injuries, including loss of teeth. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), particularly concerning torture and arbitrary treatment by State officials. The Court found that medical evidence strongly supported the Petitioner's claim, confirming serious physical harm consistent with brutal assault rather than lawful use of force. It held that the level of injury satisfied the high evidentiary threshold required for establishing violations of Article 11. The Court further ruled that State liability arises where police officers act in their official capacity, even if the individual officer is no longer available to answer proceedings. It emphasized that protection against torture is absolute and cannot be justified under investigative or custodial authority. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation for the severe and permanent injuries sustained.

In SC Application No. 186/86, the petitioner was arrested on suspicion of robbery and subjected to severe custodial torture, including hanging over a chili-smoke fire and beating with plastic pipes. Initial medical reports falsely indicated absence of injuries, while subsequent examination confirmed multiple contusions, abrasions, and fractures. The petitioner alleged manipulation of medical documentation by police influence. The Supreme Court examined violations of Article 11. It rejected the initial medical report as unreliable, noting the impossibility of accurate examination in the presence of custodial pressure. The Court held that state responsibility extends to all acts of police officers and that custodial torture constitutes a grave constitutional violation irrespective of the alleged offence of the detainee. It emphasized that constitutional protection applies even to suspected or convicted offenders. The Court found that the petitioner was subjected to torture and cruel treatment and held the State liable. Compensation and costs were awarded, reaffirming strict judicial scrutiny over custodial conduct and medical integrity in detention settings.

intake.what_happened: I am a Muslim woman who was wearing a yellow dress with a printed wheel-like design. Police came to my home after a complaint that the design looked like a Buddhist religious symbol. Even after one officer said the design was not that symbol, more police officers came, took the dress, arrested me, kept me overnight at the police station, and produced me in court on allegations connected to insulting religion and religious hatred.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, overnight police custody, remand custody for 16 days, distress, reputational harm, fear, humiliation, and criminal proceedings based on allegations that were later not pursued.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Muslim woman from the Hasalaka area. I wore a yellow dress that had a wheel-like design printed on it. A police officer came to my house and asked about the dress because someone had complained that it looked like a Buddhist religious symbol. I was told to change clothes, and the police took the dress and took me to the Hasalaka Police Station. I explained that I had received the dress as a gift while working abroad and had worn it before without any problem. My statement was recorded in Sinhala, which I do not understand properly. I was kept overnight, produced in court the next day, and remanded because the police made serious allegations connected to religion and public hatred. I believe I did not intend to insult any religion and that the police acted unfairly and without proper legal basis.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court accepted the petitioner's version over the inconsistent narratives of the 2nd respondent police officer. It held that although the dress may have offended some members of the public in the post-Easter attack context, the petitioner had not committed an offence under section 291B of the Penal Code or section 3(1) of the ICCPR Act because there was no deliberate malicious intention to insult Buddhism and no advocacy of religious hatred amounting to incitement. The arrest therefore lacked legal basis and violated Article 13(1). Because the arrest was unlawful, the ensuing police custody and deprivation of liberty also violated Article 13(2). The overall criminal justice response also denied the petitioner equality and equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the 2nd respondent infringed the petitioner's rights under Articles 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2). The 2nd respondent was directed to pay Rs. 30,000 as compensation from his personal funds within six months, and the Inspector General of Police was directed to certify that no Sri Lanka Police or police association funds were used for that payment. The petitioner was entitled to recover litigation costs from the State. The Inspector General of Police was also directed to issue a Police Order within six months, with advice from the Attorney General, on the offences under section 3(1) of the ICCPR Act and section 291B of the Penal Code and how police should enforce the law in such situations.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear unlawful arrest, unlawful custody and equal protection violation case involving police misuse of religious-insult and ICCPR allegations. Useful for testing false criminal allegation handling, post-Easter public-order sensitivity, and Article 13 overclaiming control. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of access to public places and worship
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. cases.case_name:
Suneetha Kalyani de Silva and Others v. S.J.B. Suwaris, OIC Walasmulla and
Others
cases.summary: In SC(F.R.) Application Nos. 119/2015, the petitioners, members of Jehovah's Witnesses, were engaged in peaceful religious propagation when they were confronted by a hostile mob led by a religious figure. Police intervened but instead of protecting the petitioners, detained them in a police vehicle and at the station for several hours without informing them of any charges. The respondents claimed the detention was for the petitioners' own safety. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 10, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2). It held that Article 10 protects both belief and manifestation of religion, including preaching and peaceful religious activity. The Court found that police have a constitutional duty to protect individuals exercising their rights from mob intimidation rather than detaining them to appease aggressors. It further held that detention without legal basis or procedural safeguards, even if purportedly protective, is arbitrary and unconstitutional. The Court emphasized equal protection of all religions within a secular legal framework. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and awarded compensation against both the State and the responsible officer.

cases.case_name:
Ven. Aturupalayagama Pragna Surinda Thero and Another v. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station, Minneriya and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

cases.case_name: M.J.M. Faril et al v. Bandaragama Pradeshiya Sabha et al.
cases.summary: The Petitioners, representing the Wekada Jumma Mosque, obtained approval to construct a two-storey school building and completed the ground floor. During construction of the upper floor, authorities observed deviations from the approved plan, including installation of a concrete slab rather than the approved roof structure. Local residents and Buddhist monks protested, alleging the building was being converted into a mosque. Under community pressure, the Petitioners signed an undertaking affirming the premises would be used solely as a school, after which amended plans were approved. Subsequently, police ordered suspension of construction to prevent an anticipated breach of peace arising from escalating communal tension and continued allegations of religious use. The Petitioners alleged violations of Articles 10, 12(1), and 14(1)(e), claiming interference with religious freedom and discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court held that the authorities acted lawfully to preserve public order and communal harmony. It found that evidence indicated non-compliance with the original permit and failure to obtain mandatory approval required for construction connected to religious education under applicable circulars. The Court further held that the suspension was motivated by legitimate public order concerns rather than religious or racial discrimination. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to establish arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name: Lakmali v. Gunarathne and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a pregnant woman, alleged that police officers assaulted her at Imaduwa Police Station while she was inquiring about her detained husband. She claimed she was kicked in the abdomen, arrested, and detained overnight, after which she suffered a miscarriage supported by medical evidence linking it to trauma. She alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The respondents denied wrongdoing, but the Supreme Court found the medical and clinical evidence conclusively established causation between the assault and miscarriage. It held that the use of force against a pregnant woman was grossly disproportionate, unlawful, and shocking to conscience. The Court further held that custodial violence of this nature violates the most basic principles of human dignity and equality before the law. It emphasized that police officers acting with malice outside lawful authority are personally liable for their actions. The Court found that the arrest and detention were arbitrary and unjustified, and concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated. Compensation was awarded against individual officers and partially against the State.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Suneetha Kalyani de Silva and Others v. S.J.B. Suwaris, OIC Walasmulla and
Others
stage_b_cases.summary: In SC(F.R.) Application Nos. 119/2015, the petitioners, members of Jehovah's Witnesses, were engaged in peaceful religious propagation when they were confronted by a hostile mob led by a religious figure. Police intervened but instead of protecting the petitioners, detained them in a police vehicle and at the station for several hours without informing them of any charges. The respondents claimed the detention was for the petitioners' own safety. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 10, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2). It held that Article 10 protects both belief and manifestation of religion, including preaching and peaceful religious activity. The Court found that police have a constitutional duty to protect individuals exercising their rights from mob intimidation rather than detaining them to appease aggressors. It further held that detention without legal basis or procedural safeguards, even if purportedly protective, is arbitrary and unconstitutional. The Court emphasized equal protection of all religions within a secular legal framework. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and awarded compensation against both the State and the responsible officer.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Ven. Aturupalayagama Pragna Surinda Thero and Another v. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station, Minneriya and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

stage_b_cases.case_name: M.J.M. Faril et al v. Bandaragama Pradeshiya Sabha et al.
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, representing the Wekada Jumma Mosque, obtained approval to construct a two-storey school building and completed the ground floor. During construction of the upper floor, authorities observed deviations from the approved plan, including installation of a concrete slab rather than the approved roof structure. Local residents and Buddhist monks protested, alleging the building was being converted into a mosque. Under community pressure, the Petitioners signed an undertaking affirming the premises would be used solely as a school, after which amended plans were approved. Subsequently, police ordered suspension of construction to prevent an anticipated breach of peace arising from escalating communal tension and continued allegations of religious use. The Petitioners alleged violations of Articles 10, 12(1), and 14(1)(e), claiming interference with religious freedom and discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court held that the authorities acted lawfully to preserve public order and communal harmony. It found that evidence indicated non-compliance with the original permit and failure to obtain mandatory approval required for construction connected to religious education under applicable circulars. The Court further held that the suspension was motivated by legitimate public order concerns rather than religious or racial discrimination. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to establish arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application.

retrieved_contexts: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Freedom to manifest religion or belief. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom, either by himself or in association with others, and either in public or in private, to manifest his religion or belief in worship, observance, practice and teaching.

In SC(F.R.) Application Nos. 119/2015, the petitioners, members of Jehovah's Witnesses, were engaged in peaceful religious propagation when they were confronted by a hostile mob led by a religious figure. Police intervened but instead of protecting the petitioners, detained them in a police vehicle and at the station for several hours without informing them of any charges. The respondents claimed the detention was for the petitioners' own safety. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 10, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2). It held that Article 10 protects both belief and manifestation of religion, including preaching and peaceful religious activity. The Court found that police have a constitutional duty to protect individuals exercising their rights from mob intimidation rather than detaining them to appease aggressors. It further held that detention without legal basis or procedural safeguards, even if purportedly protective, is arbitrary and unconstitutional. The Court emphasized equal protection of all religions within a secular legal framework. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and awarded compensation against both the State and the responsible officer.

The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

The Petitioners, representing the Wekada Jumma Mosque, obtained approval to construct a two-storey school building and completed the ground floor. During construction of the upper floor, authorities observed deviations from the approved plan, including installation of a concrete slab rather than the approved roof structure. Local residents and Buddhist monks protested, alleging the building was being converted into a mosque. Under community pressure, the Petitioners signed an undertaking affirming the premises would be used solely as a school, after which amended plans were approved. Subsequently, police ordered suspension of construction to prevent an anticipated breach of peace arising from escalating communal tension and continued allegations of religious use. The Petitioners alleged violations of Articles 10, 12(1), and 14(1)(e), claiming interference with religious freedom and discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court held that the authorities acted lawfully to preserve public order and communal harmony. It found that evidence indicated non-compliance with the original permit and failure to obtain mandatory approval required for construction connected to religious education under applicable circulars. The Court further held that the suspension was motivated by legitimate public order concerns rather than religious or racial discrimination. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to establish arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application.

intake.what_happened: We are police officers who were injured in the line of duty due to LTTE terrorist activities and continued serving after recovery. After our injuries, we earned promotions in the police service. A Cabinet-approved relief scheme said officers like us should have the promotions earned after injury backdated to the date of injury, and similar relief was granted to other police officers, including at least one officer in the same category. However, the authorities did not grant us the same backdated promotion relief and treated us as if we were only entitled to two salary increments.
intake.harm_suffered: Unequal treatment in police service benefits, loss of backdated promotion relief, prejudice to seniority and service entitlements, and denial of relief granted to similarly situated injured police officers.
intake.user_narrative: We are police officers who were injured while performing official duties during LTTE terrorist activities. After recovering, we continued in the police service and earned promotions. A Cabinet-approved relief scheme provided that officers who were injured and later received promotions should have their first promotion after injury backdated to the date of injury. Other police officers were given relief under this scheme, including at least one officer in the same category as us. But the authorities did not give us that relief and instead treated us as if we were only entitled to two salary increments. We believe this is unfair because we are similarly placed and should be treated the same.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged infringement of Articles 12(1) and/or 14(1)(g), but leave to proceed was granted only on Article 12(1). The Court held that the petitioners were injured police officers who had earned promotions after injury and fell within the second category of the Cabinet-approved relief scheme, which required backdating of the promotion earned after injury to the date of injury. The respondents had granted similar relief to at least one senior police officer in the same category and to other eligible officers, but denied the petitioners the same treatment without a reasonable basis. This differential treatment of similarly circumstanced officers infringed Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court directed the Inspector General of Police, the National Police Commission and the Secretary to the Ministry of Public Security to take immediate meaningful steps to backdate the first promotion earned by the petitioners after they received injuries due to LTTE terrorist activities to the date of their respective injuries, and to grant the relief within four months. No compensation was ordered, but the State was directed to pay Rs. 100,000 as costs of the application to the petitioners.

step_6.answer:
**QUESTION A — INTENT OR SYSTEMIC PATTERN:**

Based on the facts described, there appears to be a reasonable basis to suggest that the alleged act might be intentional or form part of a systemic pattern of conduct. The materials state that a Cabinet-approved relief scheme provided for backdated promotions for officers injured in the line of duty who later received promotions. It is noted that "similar relief was granted to other police officers, including at least one officer in the same category" as the petitioners. However, the authorities "did not grant us the same backdated promotion relief and treated us as if we were only entitled to two salary increments." This differential application of a specific, approved relief scheme to some officers (including those in the same category) but not to the petitioners, while providing a lesser alternative, suggests a deliberate decision to exclude the petitioners from the full relief or an inconsistent pattern in the application of the scheme.

**QUESTION B — ACTUAL HARM:**

Yes, the petitioner appears to have suffered actual, tangible harm or infringement as a direct result of the alleged act.

*   **Direct Harm:**
    *   The petitioners experienced the "loss of backdated promotion relief," which is a direct denial of a specific benefit outlined in a Cabinet-approved scheme.
    *   They were "treated... as if we were only entitled to two salary increments" instead of the more substantial backdated promotion, indicating a direct deprivation of the intended relief.
    *   There was a "denial of relief granted to similarly situated injured police officers," meaning they were directly excluded from a benefit provided to others in their category.

*   **Consequential Harm:**
    *   The petitioners suffered "unequal treatment in police service benefits," which is a broader consequence stemming from the direct denial of the backdated promotion.
    *   There was "prejudice to seniority and service entitlements," which would likely flow from not having their promotions backdated to the date of injury, potentially affecting future career progression, pension, or other service-related benefits tied to seniority.
