cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name: Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: Wijepala v. Jayawardene
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Police Sergeant, was interdicted following criminal charges but was later acquitted by a competent court. Despite reinstatement, the Police Department refused to grant back wages for the interdiction period, relying on administrative circulars. The petitioner alleged that similarly situated officers who had been acquitted were granted back pay, and that the differential treatment was arbitrary and discriminatory. The case involved Article 12(1) of the Constitution guaranteeing equality and equal protection of the law. The Supreme Court examined whether administrative discretion in granting financial benefits was exercised consistently and on rational grounds. It held that once an officer is acquitted, denial of back wages must be based on objective criteria applicable uniformly across similarly situated persons. The Court found that the respondents failed to provide any reasonable justification for treating the petitioner differently from other officers in comparable circumstances. It further held that reliance on internal circulars cannot override constitutional requirements of equal treatment where a benefit is consistently extended to others in the same category. The Court concluded that the action constituted hostile discrimination and violated the equal protection guarantee. Accordingly, it ordered payment of full back wages and emoluments for the interdiction period along with costs, reaffirming that administrative discretion must be exercised fairly, reasonably, and without arbitrariness.

retrieved_contexts: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

intake.what_happened: We are employees of the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation. The management granted promotions to a group of employees without calling applications, holding interviews, or following a transparent recruitment and promotion process. Another group of employees were given personal salary increments outside the normal annual increment scheme. We believe these benefits were given based on political affiliation and personal favoritism, while other qualified employees were denied fair and equal opportunity.
intake.harm_suffered: Unequal treatment in public corporation employment, loss of fair promotion opportunities, unfair salary and career disadvantage, and arbitrary use of public institutional power.
intake.user_narrative: We work at the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation. A group of employees were promoted to higher posts without applications being called, without interviews, and without any proper transparent process. Another group received personal salary increments outside the normal scheme. Many other employees, including us, were not given the same opportunity to compete fairly or be considered based on qualifications, experience and service. We believe these decisions were made because of political connections and favoritism, and that this unfairly affected our employment rights and career progression.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court overruled the preliminary objections on time bar, necessary parties and suppression or misrepresentation of material facts, while noting that the trade union petitioners had no locus standi but the individual petitioners could maintain the application. On the merits, the Court held that the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation, a public institution using public funds, could not make promotions and grant personal salary increments arbitrarily or on political considerations. The promotions to the 9th to 41st respondents and salary increments to the 42nd to 65th respondents were found to have been granted arbitrarily based on political affiliation, infringing the Article 12(1) rights of the 1st to 8th petitioners.
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the 1st to 7th respondents infringed the Article 12(1) rights of the 1st to 8th petitioners, declared all promotions granted to the 9th to 41st respondents and all salary increments granted to the 42nd to 65th respondents consequent to the Board decision of around 25.05.2015 null and void, awarded Rs. 480,000 total compensation to the 1st to 8th petitioners with each receiving Rs. 60,000, directed the 2nd to 7th respondents to each pay Rs. 80,000 from personal funds to the Registrar within two months, and directed the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation and its present Board to formulate an approved Scheme of Recruitment and Promotion for all posts within six months and file it in the registry with notice to the petitioners.

Useful for testing state-actor classification, time-bar handling where HRCSL complaints affected limitation, and public employment overclaiming control.     *   "in the service of any Public Corporation": The employees are stated to be working at the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation, which falls under the scope of a "Public Corporation" as mentioned in the article.

Others (Supra Grade Librarians Case)
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

cases.case_name:
Dr. C.L. Illesinghe and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration and
Home Affairs and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who were Ayurvedic Medical Officers employed on a contractual basis in the public service, sought absorption into the Sri Lanka Administrative Service or alternatively requested seniority and permanency equivalent to other public officers. The dispute arose from the operation of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Minute and the Establishments Code governing recruitment, appointment, and seniority in the public sector. The Petitioners alleged that despite their qualifications and years of service, they were unfairly denied appointment opportunities within the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, amounting to a violation of their right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Respondents maintained that recruitment and seniority decisions were governed strictly by the applicable service regulations and that the Public Service Commission had acted lawfully within those established criteria. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had occurred. The Court reasoned that the Petitioners failed to establish discriminatory treatment in comparison with similarly situated officers. It emphasized that seniority must be determined according to the date of appointment to the relevant post and that disturbing established seniority structures without legal basis would be improper. The Court also observed that some contractual claims had become moot because the relevant contracts had already expired.

cases.case_name: Kanapathipillai v. Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a Programme Producer at the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation, applied for the post of Director-Tamil Service following interviews conducted in 2005. The 4th Respondent was appointed instead. The Petitioner challenged the appointment on the basis that the selected candidate was legally disqualified from re-employment in the public service under Administrative Circular 44/90 because he had earlier retired under a voluntary retirement compensation scheme. The Petitioner further asserted that among the eligible candidates he had obtained the highest marks and was entitled to fair consideration. The Supreme Court held that the appointment violated the Petitioner's rights under Article 12(1). The Court found that the relevant administrative circular clearly prohibited the re-employment of persons who had retired under the compensation scheme and therefore the 4th Respondent was ineligible for appointment. It held that appointing a legally disqualified candidate amounted to arbitrary and unlawful administrative action that denied eligible applicants equal treatment. The Court rejected the explanation that the authorities were unaware of the 4th Respondent's retirement status, emphasizing that equality under Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary disregard of mandatory procedures and recruitment standards. While the Court nullified the impugned appointment and awarded compensation and costs to the Petitioner, it declined to appoint him directly to the post. Instead, it directed the authorities to conduct a fresh lawful selection process in accordance with established administrative policies and principles of fairness.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.
Freedom of association. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of association.
Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The Petitioner, a Programme Producer at the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation, applied for the post of Director-Tamil Service following interviews conducted in 2005. The 4th Respondent was appointed instead. The Petitioner challenged the appointment on the basis that the selected candidate was legally disqualified from re-employment in the public service under Administrative Circular 44/90 because he had earlier retired under a voluntary retirement compensation scheme. The Petitioner further asserted that among the eligible candidates he had obtained the highest marks and was entitled to fair consideration. The Supreme Court held that the appointment violated the Petitioner's rights under Article 12(1). The Court found that the relevant administrative circular clearly prohibited the re-employment of persons who had retired under the compensation scheme and therefore the 4th Respondent was ineligible for appointment. It held that appointing a legally disqualified candidate amounted to arbitrary and unlawful administrative action that denied eligible applicants equal treatment. The Court rejected the explanation that the authorities were unaware of the 4th Respondent's retirement status, emphasizing that equality under Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary disregard of mandatory procedures and recruitment standards. While the Court nullified the impugned appointment and awarded compensation and costs to the Petitioner, it declined to appoint him directly to the post. Instead, it directed the authorities to conduct a fresh lawful selection process in accordance with established administrative policies and principles of fairness.

The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

intake.incident_location: Multipurpose commercial building opposite the Magistrate's Court of Galgamuwa
intake.actor_name: Galgamuwa Pradeshiya Sabha
intake.what_happened: We are Attorneys-at-Law practicing around the Galgamuwa Magistrate's Court. A local authority constructed a multipurpose commercial building opposite the court where office rooms could be used by lawyers. We expected a proper public notice and fair opportunity to apply for those rooms, but several rooms, including the better-located rooms, were allocated to some lawyers before proper notice was given and in some cases on part payments.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of fair opportunity to obtain lawyer office accommodation near court, unequal treatment in allocation of public property, professional inconvenience, financial disadvantage, and exclusion from a transparent application process.
intake.user_narrative: We are lawyers practicing at the Galgamuwa Magistrate's Court and nearby courts. Because there was a shortage of office space, we expected to be able to apply fairly for rooms in a new commercial building opposite the court. But before proper public notice was given, some lawyers had already received rooms, including the best-located rooms, and some were allowed to reserve spaces even without paying the full required amount. When we later tried to apply, we found that the process had already favoured others. We believe the local authority did not follow a fair or transparent process when allocating these public premises.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the Galgamuwa Pradeshiya Sabha and its officials acted arbitrarily and without due process or transparency when allocating rooms in a public multipurpose commercial building. The Petitioners were similarly circumstanced with the private lawyer respondents but were denied a fair opportunity, while certain rooms had already been allocated before proper notice and on unequal payment terms. This violated Article 12(1). However, Article 14(1)(g) was rejected because the failure to obtain rooms in that building caused inconvenience but did not deprive the Petitioners of their freedom to practise as lawyers.
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that Article 12(1) was violated by the 1st to 3rd respondents, quashed and set aside the contracts entered into between the 1st respondent and the 4th to 7th and 14th respondents regarding the multipurpose commercial building, ordered any non-refundable deposits under those contracts to be returned, ordered the 1st respondent to pay Rs. 10,000 compensation to each petitioner within three months, and directed CIABOC to investigate the failure of the 1st to 3rd respondents to follow due procurement process.
gold.evaluation_notes: Partial-violation local government public-property allocation case. Useful for testing Article 12(1) arbitrary administrative action and rejected Article 14(1)(g) overclaiming, because professional inconvenience was not treated as loss of freedom to engage in occupation. retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. cases.case_name: Roberts and Another v. Ratnayake and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners held municipal tenancies and leases for business stalls which were terminated by the Kandy Municipal Council on grounds of unauthorized structural alterations and residential use of commercial premises. They alleged unequal treatment compared to other stallholders who committed similar by-law breaches but were not terminated, invoking Article 12(1) on equality and equal protection. The State contended that termination was lawful due to contractual breaches and municipal by-laws. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were not similarly circumstanced to the other tenants as they had committed both by-law violations and breaches of tenancy agreements. It further held that enforcement of contractual terms does not automatically amount to infringement of fundamental rights unless constitutional arbitrariness is established. The Court found that lawful termination of tenancy under contractual and statutory authority could not be challenged as discriminatory absent proof of identical circumstances and irrational differentiation. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to discharge the burden of proving unequal treatment under Article 12(1), and therefore no fundamental rights violation was established. The application was dismissed.

cases.case_name:
Don Piyasena Karunaratne and Others v. Anuradhapura Municipal Council and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, former occupants of Municipal Council staff quarters, sought transfer of ownership of the houses they had occupied for several decades, relying on a rent-purchase claim and a ministerial direction asserting a long-term expectation of ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal treatment in denial of property transfer. The Respondents argued that the premises were staff quarters not eligible for conversion and that statutory provisions under the housing legislation restricted ownership transfer based on rent thresholds, which the Petitioners exceeded. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were legally ineligible under the governing statutory framework, particularly Section 5(A), which imposed strict eligibility conditions. It further found that the agreements constituted tenancy arrangements rather than enforceable rent-purchase contracts capable of creating ownership rights. The Court also held that no legitimate expectation arose because the Council had made no binding promise but only indicated discretionary future consideration. Accordingly, it concluded that there was no arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application for failure to establish a constitutional violation.

cases.case_name:
D. Wathsala Subhashini De Silva and Another v. Hasitha Kesara Wettimuni and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged the denial of school admission under a proximity-based quota system, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The authorities rejected admission to Grade 1 at a national school despite ownership of the residential premises and supporting utility documentation. The dispute centered on whether authorities could distinguish between two houses within the same family compound for proximity calculation purposes. The respondents argued that the application was based on incorrect residency representation and that the relevant assessment should be made from the actual occupied house used for residence. The Supreme Court held that where a family owns an entire property compound and no competing occupancy exists, school authorities cannot arbitrarily distinguish between buildings within the same premises for admission assessment. It found that the rejection was based on an unjustified investigative approach that treated internal residential arrangement as determinative. The Court emphasized that documentary evidence already supported the petitioners' residence claim and that authorities had no basis to override ownership and occupancy facts. It concluded that the denial of admission was arbitrary and amounted to unequal treatment under Article 12(1). The Court declared a violation and ordered immediate admission of the child.

cases.case_name: Viraj Priyankara Abeyratne v. Ceylon Electricity Board and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Viraj Priyankara Abeyratne v. Ceylon Electricity Board and Others challenged the arbitrary conversion of a privately constructed road into a public road in Tangalle to facilitate an electricity connection for an adjacent occupier. The 8th respondent certified the road as public within a highly expedited timeframe, enabling installation of electricity infrastructure across the petitioner's land despite his objections. The statutory framework under the Electricity Act required a mandatory inquiry by the Divisional Secretary within six weeks where objections to way-leave access were raised, but this procedure was bypassed. The petitioner alleged violations of Article 12(1) and interference with lawful economic activity. The respondents defended the actions as administrative necessity. The Supreme Court examined whether the decision-making process was arbitrary and whether statutory safeguards had been deliberately circumvented. It held that the coordinated and expedited actions of multiple officials demonstrated deliberate arbitrariness rather than administrative error. The Court found evidence of collusion and concluded that the petitioner was denied a legally mandated inquiry process available to all similarly situated persons. It held that such selective deprivation of statutory protection violated equality before the law. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), quashed the administrative decision, and imposed personal liability on the responsible officials for damages.

cases.case_name: Dharmarathne and Others v. Divisional Secretary, Udapalatha
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged prolonged administrative confusion regarding the territorial boundaries and jurisdictional authority of their village, resulting in repeated referrals between local authorities without final resolution. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal and inconsistent administrative treatment. The respondents contended that the issue arose from technical boundary ambiguities requiring determination by competent delimitation authorities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the hardship faced by the petitioners but held that the matter constituted an administrative boundary dispute rather than a deliberate infringement of fundamental rights. It found no evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal treatment targeted at the petitioners. However, the Court observed systemic delays and lack of coordination between relevant authorities. It directed the Divisional Secretary and Surveyor General to take steps to expedite submission of recommendations to the National Delimitation Commission for resolution of the boundary issue. The Court concluded that while no fundamental rights violation was established, the petitioners were entitled to administrative resolution of their grievance.

retrieved_contexts: Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Restrictions on freedom of movement and residence. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(h) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The petitioner in Viraj Priyankara Abeyratne v. Ceylon Electricity Board and Others challenged the arbitrary conversion of a privately constructed road into a public road in Tangalle to facilitate an electricity connection for an adjacent occupier. The 8th respondent certified the road as public within a highly expedited timeframe, enabling installation of electricity infrastructure across the petitioner's land despite his objections. The statutory framework under the Electricity Act required a mandatory inquiry by the Divisional Secretary within six weeks where objections to way-leave access were raised, but this procedure was bypassed. The petitioner alleged violations of Article 12(1) and interference with lawful economic activity. The respondents defended the actions as administrative necessity. The Supreme Court examined whether the decision-making process was arbitrary and whether statutory safeguards had been deliberately circumvented. It held that the coordinated and expedited actions of multiple officials demonstrated deliberate arbitrariness rather than administrative error. The Court found evidence of collusion and concluded that the petitioner was denied a legally mandated inquiry process available to all similarly situated persons. It held that such selective deprivation of statutory protection violated equality before the law. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), quashed the administrative decision, and imposed personal liability on the responsible officials for damages.

The Petitioners held municipal tenancies and leases for business stalls which were terminated by the Kandy Municipal Council on grounds of unauthorized structural alterations and residential use of commercial premises. They alleged unequal treatment compared to other stallholders who committed similar by-law breaches but were not terminated, invoking Article 12(1) on equality and equal protection. The State contended that termination was lawful due to contractual breaches and municipal by-laws. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were not similarly circumstanced to the other tenants as they had committed both by-law violations and breaches of tenancy agreements. It further held that enforcement of contractual terms does not automatically amount to infringement of fundamental rights unless constitutional arbitrariness is established. The Court found that lawful termination of tenancy under contractual and statutory authority could not be challenged as discriminatory absent proof of identical circumstances and irrational differentiation. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to discharge the burden of proving unequal treatment under Article 12(1), and therefore no fundamental rights violation was established. The application was dismissed.

The Petitioners, former occupants of Municipal Council staff quarters, sought transfer of ownership of the houses they had occupied for several decades, relying on a rent-purchase claim and a ministerial direction asserting a long-term expectation of ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal treatment in denial of property transfer. The Respondents argued that the premises were staff quarters not eligible for conversion and that statutory provisions under the housing legislation restricted ownership transfer based on rent thresholds, which the Petitioners exceeded. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were legally ineligible under the governing statutory framework, particularly Section 5(A), which imposed strict eligibility conditions. It further found that the agreements constituted tenancy arrangements rather than enforceable rent-purchase contracts capable of creating ownership rights. The Court also held that no legitimate expectation arose because the Council had made no binding promise but only indicated discretionary future consideration. Accordingly, it concluded that there was no arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application for failure to establish a constitutional violation.

intake.incident_location: Hatharaliyadda Police Station and Galagedera area
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Hatharaliyadda Police Station
intake.what_happened: My minor son, who had just completed his Ordinary Level examination, was taken by police in connection with an alleged jewellery theft from a relative's house. He was arrested without a proper basis, kept at the police station before being produced in court, beaten on the soles of his feet with a pole during questioning, and had nai miris extract put into his eyes. When I went to the police station, I was not allowed proper access to him and heard him crying out for help.
intake.harm_suffered: Physical torture of a minor, pain and injuries to the soles of the feet, burning and fear from chilli extract being put into the eyes, unlawful arrest, delayed production before a Magistrate, detention with an adult detainee, psychological trauma to the child, and severe emotional distress to the mother.
intake.user_narrative: My son is a minor and was a school student who had just finished his O/L exam. Police suspected him in relation to jewellery allegedly stolen from a relative's house. He was taken to the Hatharaliyadda Police Station even though there was no proper evidence against him. During questioning, a police officer beat the soles of his feet with a pole and later put nai miris extract into his eyes. I went to the police station to see him, but I was not properly allowed to be with him, and I heard him calling out for me to save him. He was kept in custody and produced before court only later. This caused my son physical and mental suffering and caused me extreme distress as his mother.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the 1st petitioner, a minor, was tortured by the 1st respondent police officer through beatings to the soles of his feet and the pouring of nai miris extract into his eyes, with medical evidence corroborating injuries to the soles. The Court also held that the arrest was not based on reasonable suspicion or lawful procedure, and that the minor was not produced before the Magistrate within the required time, violating Articles 13(1) and 13(2). Since those violations also denied equal protection of the law, Article 12(1) was infringed. The Court further held that the 2nd petitioner mother was subjected to mental torture when she was denied access to her minor son and heard him calling for help while in police custody.
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the 1st respondent infringed the 1st petitioner's rights under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2), and infringed the 2nd petitioner's rights under Article 11. The 1st respondent was ordered to pay Rs. 300,000 from his personal funds to the 1st petitioner and Rs. 75,000 from his personal funds to the 2nd petitioner. The Inspector General of Police was directed to issue directions to all police officers requiring that when a minor is arrested, the mother, father or close relative be granted access before production before the Magistrate and in any event within six hours of arrest.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear police torture, unlawful arrest and delayed production case involving a minor detainee and the mother's mental torture claim. Useful for testing Article 11 physical and psychological harm, minor arrest safeguards, and Articles 13(1), 13(2) and 12(1) together. cases.case_name: Rathnayake Wijesiri v. Rohan Fernando and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested by police on suspicion of involvement in a jewellery robbery and detained for several days without production before a Magistrate. During custody, he alleged severe torture including suspension by the hands, beating with a club, and application of chili powder to sensitive areas to extract a confession. Medical evidence supported the presence of injuries consistent with custodial abuse. The case concerned Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Supreme Court evaluated whether the conduct of police officers met the constitutional threshold of severity. It held that custodial torture designed to extract confessions constitutes a grave violation of absolute constitutional rights. The Court placed significant weight on medical findings corroborating the petitioner's version and rejected blanket denials by the respondents. It further held that systematic physical abuse for investigative purposes is incompatible with constitutional protections and cannot be justified under any circumstances. The Court concluded that Article 11 had been violated by multiple officers involved in the detention and interrogation. It ordered compensation and costs, including personal liability for the Officer-in-Charge, reaffirming strict constitutional prohibition against custodial violence.

cases.case_name: Hapugodage Jagath Perera v. Gothami Ranasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested following a land dispute and alleged that while in police custody he was subjected to severe assault resulting in permanent injuries, including loss of teeth. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), particularly concerning torture and arbitrary treatment by State officials. The Court found that medical evidence strongly supported the Petitioner's claim, confirming serious physical harm consistent with brutal assault rather than lawful use of force. It held that the level of injury satisfied the high evidentiary threshold required for establishing violations of Article 11. The Court further ruled that State liability arises where police officers act in their official capacity, even if the individual officer is no longer available to answer proceedings. It emphasized that protection against torture is absolute and cannot be justified under investigative or custodial authority. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation for the severe and permanent injuries sustained.

It also imposed personal liability on the officers involved, reinforcing accountability for State agents. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and awarded compensation.

Herath Mudiyanselage Indika Kanchana Hemantha v. Karunaratne
Mudiyanselage Abeysinghe and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested on 26 June 2012 by police officers attached to the Maho Police Station in connection with an alleged train bag theft. He alleged that during custody he was suspended by his hands from a roof, beaten with a wooden pole, and assaulted on the soles of his feet while officers stood on his knees. The police denied the arrest to family members and kept him outside formal custody until he was placed in a cell on 28 June and produced before a Magistrate on 29 June. Although an initial medical report from Maho Hospital recorded no injuries, a later Judicial Medical Officer's examination confirmed multiple injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. The Petitioner was also not identified by witnesses at an identification parade. Invoking Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2), he alleged torture, arbitrary arrest, and unlawful detention. The Court held that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's fundamental rights. It rejected the earlier hospital report as unreliable because it contradicted the detailed findings of the Judicial Medical Officer and appeared suspiciously superficial. The Court further found that the police version regarding the date of arrest was fabricated and unsupported by the medical evidence. Liability was imposed not only on the officers directly involved but also on superior officers who failed in their duty to supervise subordinates and ensure humane treatment of detainees. Compensation was awarded against the individual officers and the State.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Rathnayake Wijesiri v. Rohan Fernando and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested by police on suspicion of involvement in a jewellery robbery and detained for several days without production before a Magistrate. During custody, he alleged severe torture including suspension by the hands, beating with a club, and application of chili powder to sensitive areas to extract a confession. Medical evidence supported the presence of injuries consistent with custodial abuse. The case concerned Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Supreme Court evaluated whether the conduct of police officers met the constitutional threshold of severity. It held that custodial torture designed to extract confessions constitutes a grave violation of absolute constitutional rights. The Court placed significant weight on medical findings corroborating the petitioner's version and rejected blanket denials by the respondents. It further held that systematic physical abuse for investigative purposes is incompatible with constitutional protections and cannot be justified under any circumstances. The Court concluded that Article 11 had been violated by multiple officers involved in the detention and interrogation. It ordered compensation and costs, including personal liability for the Officer-in-Charge, reaffirming strict constitutional prohibition against custodial violence.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Hapugodage Jagath Perera v. Gothami Ranasinghe and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested following a land dispute and alleged that while in police custody he was subjected to severe assault resulting in permanent injuries, including loss of teeth. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), particularly concerning torture and arbitrary treatment by State officials. The Court found that medical evidence strongly supported the Petitioner's claim, confirming serious physical harm consistent with brutal assault rather than lawful use of force. It held that the level of injury satisfied the high evidentiary threshold required for establishing violations of Article 11. The Court further ruled that State liability arises where police officers act in their official capacity, even if the individual officer is no longer available to answer proceedings. It emphasized that protection against torture is absolute and cannot be justified under investigative or custodial authority. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation for the severe and permanent injuries sustained.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

The petitioner was arrested by police on suspicion of involvement in a jewellery robbery and detained for several days without production before a Magistrate. During custody, he alleged severe torture including suspension by the hands, beating with a club, and application of chili powder to sensitive areas to extract a confession. Medical evidence supported the presence of injuries consistent with custodial abuse. The case concerned Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Supreme Court evaluated whether the conduct of police officers met the constitutional threshold of severity. It held that custodial torture designed to extract confessions constitutes a grave violation of absolute constitutional rights. The Court placed significant weight on medical findings corroborating the petitioner's version and rejected blanket denials by the respondents. It further held that systematic physical abuse for investigative purposes is incompatible with constitutional protections and cannot be justified under any circumstances. The Court concluded that Article 11 had been violated by multiple officers involved in the detention and interrogation. It ordered compensation and costs, including personal liability for the Officer-in-Charge, reaffirming strict constitutional prohibition against custodial violence.

The Petitioner was arrested following a land dispute and alleged that while in police custody he was subjected to severe assault resulting in permanent injuries, including loss of teeth. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), particularly concerning torture and arbitrary treatment by State officials. The Court found that medical evidence strongly supported the Petitioner's claim, confirming serious physical harm consistent with brutal assault rather than lawful use of force. It held that the level of injury satisfied the high evidentiary threshold required for establishing violations of Article 11. The Court further ruled that State liability arises where police officers act in their official capacity, even if the individual officer is no longer available to answer proceedings. It emphasized that protection against torture is absolute and cannot be justified under investigative or custodial authority. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation for the severe and permanent injuries sustained.

intake.what_happened: I had a personal dispute with a journalist friend who had borrowed money from me and failed to repay it. After our friendship broke down, he complained to the police that I had poisoned his well. I was summoned to the Thihagoda Police Station, publicly accused and distressed, and later facts were reported to court against me. A Government Analyst report on the water sample was negative, and the Police Commission recommended disciplinary action against the police officers and termination of the criminal proceedings, but the police continued summoning me and referred me to the Mediation Board.
intake.harm_suffered: Police harassment, public humiliation, distress, criminal proceedings based on an unsupported complaint, repeated police summons, reputational harm, and denial of fair police treatment.
intake.user_narrative: I am a social service activist. A journalist who had been my friend borrowed a large amount of money from me, but later failed to repay it. After I stopped lending him money, our relationship became bad and he complained to the police that I had poisoned his well. I was called to the Thihagoda Police Station, where I was shown to others and accused in a humiliating way. Later I found that facts had been reported to court against me. The water sample report was negative and I complained to the Police Commission. Even after recommendations were made that action should be taken against the officers and that the criminal case should end, the police kept summoning me and told me to go before the Mediation Board. I believe the police acted unfairly, unreasonably and in a biased way because of the false complaint made against me.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the 1st and 2nd respondents acted arbitrarily, unreasonably and discriminatorily in handling the complaint against the petitioner. They reported the matter to court without a proper investigation, continued to summon the petitioner and refer her to the police and Mediation Board despite the Government Analyst's negative report and the directions of the National Police Commission, and failed to act properly on the false allegations. This conduct violated the petitioner's Article 12(1) right to equality and equal protection of the law.
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the 1st and 2nd respondents violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1). As the 2nd respondent had passed away, no relief was granted against him. Against the 1st respondent, the Court directed the National Police Commission and the Deputy Inspector General of Police of the Matara-Hambantota Division to conduct a thorough disciplinary inquiry and take action accordingly.
