cases.case_name:
Chaminda Sampath Kumara Wickremapathirana v. Sub Inspector Salwatura and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a labourer, was arrested on May 20, 2009, by police officers while returning home carrying chicken meat. Police officers searched his residence without a warrant and seized pawning receipts belonging to third parties. He was detained at the Bandaragama Police Station for seven days before being produced before a Magistrate. During custody, the Petitioner was stripped, beaten with clubs and hose pipes, and forced to consume bird's eye chilies. Crushed chilies were also poured into his eyes and nose while he was restrained in painful positions. The Officer-in-Charge later falsely recorded the date of arrest as May 26 in an attempt to conceal the unlawful delay in producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate. The Petitioner was eventually acquitted of theft charges because of absence of evidence. Alleging violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), the Petitioner challenged the conduct of the Respondents. The Supreme Court accepted the Petitioner's testimony and observed that methods such as the use of chilies and hose pipes are specifically intended to inflict suffering while minimizing visible physical marks. Hospital records corroborated injuries to the wrists and ankles consistent with suspension and assault. The Court held that the torture inflicted caused both physical and enduring psychological harm and that the Officer-in-Charge bore responsibility for permitting the police station to be used for unlawful acts. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated and awarded compensation against both the officers and the State.

cases.case_name: CH.A. Manoj Talis v. Inspector Hiriyadeniya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya
Police Station and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya Police Station and Others arose from an incident on 17 August 2017 during the arrest of the petitioner's daughter by police officers. The petitioner alleged that she intervened and was subjected to severe assault including slapping, kicking, trampling, and threats of being shot, resulting in humiliation and physical harm. The respondents contended that she obstructed a lawful arrest and sustained no assault, claiming any injury was self-inflicted during resistance. Medical evidence from Kandy Teaching Hospital recorded no injuries, with scans and X-rays showing normal results. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1). The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture require proof to a high degree of probability supported by credible medical evidence. It found the absence of injuries in medical reports inconsistent with the alleged severe assault. The Court also considered inconsistencies in witness statements and noted that the petitioner sought legal advice before medical treatment, which undermined her account of severe trauma. It further observed that internal police inquiries had been conducted into the complaint. Accordingly, the Court held that the petitioner failed to establish any constitutional violation and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Roshan Mahesh Ukwatta v Sub Inspector Marasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested at his residence on 22 February 2006 by officers attached to the Welikada Police Station. While in police custody he was subjected to severe torture. His hands and legs were tied together, an iron rod was inserted between his elbows and knees, and he was suspended and beaten with batons and poles. He was produced before a Magistrate only on 28 February 2006, six days after the arrest. Medical evidence confirmed nineteen injuries including a fractured jaw, a perforated eardrum, and a dislocated joint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(2) of the Constitution. The respondents denied the allegations and claimed that the petitioner had been arrested on 27 February 2006 and injured after falling from a wall. The Supreme Court rejected the police version and found that official records had been falsified. A complaint made to the Human Rights Commission on 24 February established that the petitioner had already been detained by that date. The Court further held that the severity of the injuries was inconsistent with the explanation offered by the police. The 2nd respondent, as Officer-in-Charge, was found liable for culpable inaction and complicity because he failed to supervise subordinates and facilitated falsification of official records. The Court declared that Articles 11 and 13(2) had been violated and awarded compensation and costs against the State.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

The Petitioner, a labourer, was arrested on May 20, 2009, by police officers while returning home carrying chicken meat. Police officers searched his residence without a warrant and seized pawning receipts belonging to third parties. He was detained at the Bandaragama Police Station for seven days before being produced before a Magistrate. During custody, the Petitioner was stripped, beaten with clubs and hose pipes, and forced to consume bird's eye chilies. Crushed chilies were also poured into his eyes and nose while he was restrained in painful positions. The Officer-in-Charge later falsely recorded the date of arrest as May 26 in an attempt to conceal the unlawful delay in producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate. The Petitioner was eventually acquitted of theft charges because of absence of evidence. Alleging violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), the Petitioner challenged the conduct of the Respondents. The Supreme Court accepted the Petitioner's testimony and observed that methods such as the use of chilies and hose pipes are specifically intended to inflict suffering while minimizing visible physical marks. Hospital records corroborated injuries to the wrists and ankles consistent with suspension and assault. The Court held that the torture inflicted caused both physical and enduring psychological harm and that the Officer-in-Charge bore responsibility for permitting the police station to be used for unlawful acts. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated and awarded compensation against both the officers and the State.

The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya Police Station and Others arose from an incident on 17 August 2017 during the arrest of the petitioner's daughter by police officers. The petitioner alleged that she intervened and was subjected to severe assault including slapping, kicking, trampling, and threats of being shot, resulting in humiliation and physical harm. The respondents contended that she obstructed a lawful arrest and sustained no assault, claiming any injury was self-inflicted during resistance. Medical evidence from Kandy Teaching Hospital recorded no injuries, with scans and X-rays showing normal results. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1). The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture require proof to a high degree of probability supported by credible medical evidence. It found the absence of injuries in medical reports inconsistent with the alleged severe assault. The Court also considered inconsistencies in witness statements and noted that the petitioner sought legal advice before medical treatment, which undermined her account of severe trauma. intake.user_narrative: I operate buses between Colombo and Kottawa. One night I was returning home when I saw my two buses parked after the day's running. A police officer abused me, pointed a pistol at my head and threatened to kill me. Other officers came, slapped me, made me kneel and beat me inside my own bus while I was handcuffed. My wife, mother and others pleaded with them to stop, but they continued. I was taken to the Kottawa Police Station, assaulted again, and placed in a cell. The next day I was produced before court on a heroin possession allegation, which I completely deny. My lawyer told court about my injuries, but I was not properly taken before the judicial medical officer at first. Later a medical report recorded injuries to my face, chest, forearms and wrist. I believe the police assaulted me and then made a false drug case to cover it up.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court found that the petitioner was assaulted by police officers while handcuffed, with multiple affidavits and the second judicial medical report corroborating injuries to his face, chest, forearms and wrist. The assault by the 2nd and 3rd respondents amounted to torture or cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 11, while the other police officers bore responsibility for failing to prevent or rectify the violations. The failure to properly produce the petitioner before a judicial medical officer violated Article 12(1), and the arrest and detention without properly informing him of the reasons for arrest violated Article 13(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 11, 12(1) and 13(1) were violated by the 1st to 6th respondents. Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000 was awarded to the petitioner, to be paid jointly by the 1st to 6th respondents from their personal funds.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

cases.case_name:
K.H.G. Kushan Indika v. Christy Leonard Ranjan Wijesekera, OIC Pitigala and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, employed as a driver for the Sri Lanka State Plantation Corporation, was waiting at a bus halt on April 2, 2007 when a police jeep arrived and the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Pitigala Police Station, questioned him. Although the Petitioner produced his driving licence as identification, the 1st Respondent assaulted him by slapping him repeatedly and compelled him to load a heavy motorbike into a truck. When the Petitioner requested assistance, the 1st Respondent assaulted him with a club several times. The Petitioner was then taken to the police station, detained in a cell for nearly two hours, and released without any statement being recorded or charges being filed. The Respondent attempted to justify the arrest on the basis of suspicious conduct. The Court held that no reasonable suspicion existed to support the arrest and clarified that a driving licence constituted valid identification. The Court determined that the public assault, forced labour, and unlawful detention subjected the Petitioner to degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 11, notwithstanding the non-grievous nature of the injuries. The Court further held that the failure to provide reasons for arrest or record a statement constituted a serious procedural lapse. The Supreme Court concluded that Articles 11 and 13(1) had been violated and directed the 1st Respondent to personally compensate the Petitioner.

cases.case_name: Sri Thaminda, Dharshane and Mahalekam v. Inspector of Police and Others
cases.summary: During a festival on August 11, 2003, the three Petitioners, who were intoxicated, became involved in a confrontation with police officers regarding the parking of a three-wheeler. A scuffle followed during which a Police Constable was injured and hospitalized. The Petitioners were arrested and later sustained multiple injuries. They alleged that police officers and members of the Rapid Deployment Force assaulted them while in custody, amounting to cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11. The Respondents contended that the injuries resulted from an angry crowd attempting to rescue the injured constable and denied responsibility for the assaults. The Supreme Court held that the arrests themselves were justified because the Petitioners had behaved aggressively and police intervention was necessary to prevent escalation of violence and maintain public order. Consequently, no violation of Article 13(1) was established. However, the Court found sufficient material to conclude that the Petitioners were assaulted by state officers acting under colour of office. The Court reaffirmed that constitutional protection against torture and cruel or degrading treatment applies irrespective of the victim's conduct. Nevertheless, the Court declined to award compensation because the Petitioners had themselves behaved in a disorderly and disgraceful manner and contributed to the circumstances leading to the incident. Declaratory relief alone was therefore granted for the infringement of Article 11.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

stage_b_cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

intake.incident_location: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Belihul Oya
intake.actor_name: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and University Grants Commission
intake.actor_role: public university officials and higher education authorities
intake.what_happened: I applied for an advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post at Sabaragamuwa University and was appointed as a Lecturer (Probationary) on the understanding that I would be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II after the necessary approval. I accepted the appointment and joined the university, but the authorities failed for years to regularize me into the advertised post despite my qualifications, internal committee recommendations, Council consideration, and an order of the University Services Appeals Board.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of proper academic designation, delayed career progression, loss of salary entitlements, increments, sabbatical leave, professional recognition and academic opportunities.
intake.user_narrative: I applied for an advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post at Sabaragamuwa University. Instead, I was appointed as a Lecturer (Probationary), but the appointment letter indicated that I would later be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II after the required approval. I accepted the post and moved from another senior public research position because I expected better academic career prospects. For many years, I repeatedly asked the university and the University Grants Commission to correct my appointment. Internal university bodies later recognized that a mistake had been made, and the University Services Appeals Board also recommended that I be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II from my initial appointment date. Even after that, the authorities did not implement the recommendation, causing loss of salary benefits, sabbatical leave and professional opportunities.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the petitioner had applied for the advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post but was appointed to a non-advertised Lecturer (Probationary) post with an assurance of later placement as Senior Lecturer Grade II. Internal university committees, the University Council and the University Services Appeals Board recognized the administrative error and recommended rectification, but the university and UGC failed to implement those recommendations. This administrative inaction, procedural irregularity and denial of the petitioner's proper academic position and entitlements violated Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the 1st and 27th respondents collectively violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The 1st respondent was directed to immediately implement the University Services Appeals Board order dated 26.10.2022 and place the petitioner in the position of Senior Lecturer Grade II with effect from 06.04.2009, together with salary entitlements due for that post. No compensation was ordered because the petitioner had been employed in a different capacity in the same institution.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear public university employment and academic career progression case involving administrative inaction, legitimate expectation, and failure to implement USAB recommendations. retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The actions of a public university and the University Grants Commission in an employment matter fall under the purview of executive or administrative action.

Therefore, based on the materials provided, the alleged violation appears to be **(a) A DIRECT act by a state authority acting in official capacity**. retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment under existing written law
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

cases.case_name: Ananda Dharmadasa and Others v. Ariyaratne Hewage and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, former educational officers, challenged their exclusion from appointment to the Sri Lanka Educational Administrative Service despite earlier Cabinet decisions permitting absorption of officers performing in scheduled posts. They alleged unequal treatment under Article 12(1), arguing that similarly situated officers were appointed while they were excluded without justification. The State raised preliminary objections including delay and ineligibility based on qualification criteria. The Supreme Court held that constitutional relief under Article 126 must be sought within one month of the alleged infringement and that prolonged delay rendered the application time-barred. On merits, the Court found that equality requires comparability of circumstances, and the Petitioners failed to demonstrate that they satisfied the mandatory qualifications required for appointment. It further held that valid administrative classification based on objective criteria does not amount to discrimination. The Court emphasized that unequal treatment must be shown in identical circumstances without rational basis, which was not established in this case. It concluded that there was no violation of Article 12(1) and dismissed the application on both procedural and substantive grounds.

cases.case_name:
Dr. C.L. Illesinghe and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration and
Home Affairs and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who were Ayurvedic Medical Officers employed on a contractual basis in the public service, sought absorption into the Sri Lanka Administrative Service or alternatively requested seniority and permanency equivalent to other public officers. The dispute arose from the operation of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Minute and the Establishments Code governing recruitment, appointment, and seniority in the public sector. The Petitioners alleged that despite their qualifications and years of service, they were unfairly denied appointment opportunities within the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, amounting to a violation of their right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Respondents maintained that recruitment and seniority decisions were governed strictly by the applicable service regulations and that the Public Service Commission had acted lawfully within those established criteria. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had occurred. The Court reasoned that the Petitioners failed to establish discriminatory treatment in comparison with similarly situated officers. It emphasized that seniority must be determined according to the date of appointment to the relevant post and that disturbing established seniority structures without legal basis would be improper. The Court also observed that some contractual claims had become moot because the relevant contracts had already expired.

cases.case_name:
Harshani S. Siriwardana v. Malsiri J. Seneviratne, Secretary, Ministry of Health
(Western Province) and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner applied for the post of Social Service Officer in the Western Province pursuant to a Gazette notification issued in 2007. She attended an interview, produced her academic certificates, and was subsequently selected and issued with an appointment letter. Thereafter, the 1st Respondent informed her that her Bachelor of Arts General Degree did not satisfy the recruitment requirement specifying qualifications in Sociology or Economics. Consequently, the authorities cancelled her appointment. The Petitioner challenged the cancellation under Article 12(1), relying primarily on the doctrine of legitimate expectation and contending that the authorities could not revoke an appointment after formally selecting her. The Court examined the recruitment criteria contained in the Gazette notification and held that the prescribed qualifications expressly required a degree specializing in Sociology or Economics. Since the Petitioner possessed only a general arts degree, the Court found that she did not satisfy the mandatory eligibility criteria for the post. The Court further held that the doctrine of legitimate expectation cannot compel a public authority to perpetuate an illegality or act contrary to lawfully established recruitment requirements. It reasoned that the initial appointment resulted from an administrative error which the State was entitled to correct in the interests of legality and proper administration. The Court concluded that the cancellation was based upon an objective evaluation of qualifications and did not constitute arbitrary or discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court therefore held that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application without costs.

cases.case_name: M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others challenged the denial of admission to the Faculty of Law despite having obtained three A passes and a competitive Z-score in the GCE Advanced Level examination. The University Grants Commission rejected his application on the basis that he was allegedly registered for a Higher National Diploma at an Advanced Technological Institute, which under admission rules disqualified him from university entry unless formally withdrawn. The petitioner contended that he was never validly registered due to failure to submit mandatory documents and absence of attendance, and that the registration entry was a clerical error. The respondents relied on institutional records indicating active registration status. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court examined whether administrative error could lawfully be used to deny merit-based university admission. It held that the petitioner was not validly registered under the applicable procedural requirements and that the State institution's clerical mistake could not prejudice his educational rights. The Court further held that denial of admission to a qualified student on the basis of erroneous data constituted arbitrary state action contrary to equality principles. It emphasised the State's obligation to ensure fair and non-arbitrary access to higher education. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), set aside the decision, and granted relief restoring the petitioner's eligibility.

stage_b_cases.case_name: M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner in M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others challenged the denial of admission to the Faculty of Law despite having obtained three A passes and a competitive Z-score in the GCE Advanced Level examination. The University Grants Commission rejected his application on the basis that he was allegedly registered for a Higher National Diploma at an Advanced Technological Institute, which under admission rules disqualified him from university entry unless formally withdrawn. The petitioner contended that he was never validly registered due to failure to submit mandatory documents and absence of attendance, and that the registration entry was a clerical error. The respondents relied on institutional records indicating active registration status. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court examined whether administrative error could lawfully be used to deny merit-based university admission. It held that the petitioner was not validly registered under the applicable procedural requirements and that the State institution's clerical mistake could not prejudice his educational rights. The Court further held that denial of admission to a qualified student on the basis of erroneous data constituted arbitrary state action contrary to equality principles. It emphasised the State's obligation to ensure fair and non-arbitrary access to higher education. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), set aside the decision, and granted relief restoring the petitioner's eligibility.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Ananda Dharmadasa and Others v. Ariyaratne Hewage and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, former educational officers, challenged their exclusion from appointment to the Sri Lanka Educational Administrative Service despite earlier Cabinet decisions permitting absorption of officers performing in scheduled posts. They alleged unequal treatment under Article 12(1), arguing that similarly situated officers were appointed while they were excluded without justification. The State raised preliminary objections including delay and ineligibility based on qualification criteria. The Supreme Court held that constitutional relief under Article 126 must be sought within one month of the alleged infringement and that prolonged delay rendered the application time-barred. On merits, the Court found that equality requires comparability of circumstances, and the Petitioners failed to demonstrate that they satisfied the mandatory qualifications required for appointment. It further held that valid administrative classification based on objective criteria does not amount to discrimination. The Court emphasized that unequal treatment must be shown in identical circumstances without rational basis, which was not established in this case. It concluded that there was no violation of Article 12(1) and dismissed the application on both procedural and substantive grounds.

retrieved_contexts: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The petitioner in M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others challenged the denial of admission to the Faculty of Law despite having obtained three A passes and a competitive Z-score in the GCE Advanced Level examination. The University Grants Commission rejected his application on the basis that he was allegedly registered for a Higher National Diploma at an Advanced Technological Institute, which under admission rules disqualified him from university entry unless formally withdrawn. The petitioner contended that he was never validly registered due to failure to submit mandatory documents and absence of attendance, and that the registration entry was a clerical error. The respondents relied on institutional records indicating active registration status. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court examined whether administrative error could lawfully be used to deny merit-based university admission. It held that the petitioner was not validly registered under the applicable procedural requirements and that the State institution's clerical mistake could not prejudice his educational rights. The Court further held that denial of admission to a qualified student on the basis of erroneous data constituted arbitrary state action contrary to equality principles. It emphasised the State's obligation to ensure fair and non-arbitrary access to higher education. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), set aside the decision, and granted relief restoring the petitioner's eligibility.

The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

The Petitioners, former educational officers, challenged their exclusion from appointment to the Sri Lanka Educational Administrative Service despite earlier Cabinet decisions permitting absorption of officers performing in scheduled posts. They alleged unequal treatment under Article 12(1), arguing that similarly situated officers were appointed while they were excluded without justification. The State raised preliminary objections including delay and ineligibility based on qualification criteria. The Supreme Court held that constitutional relief under Article 126 must be sought within one month of the alleged infringement and that prolonged delay rendered the application time-barred. On merits, the Court found that equality requires comparability of circumstances, and the Petitioners failed to demonstrate that they satisfied the mandatory qualifications required for appointment. It further held that valid administrative classification based on objective criteria does not amount to discrimination. The Court emphasized that unequal treatment must be shown in identical circumstances without rational basis, which was not established in this case. It concluded that there was no violation of Article 12(1) and dismissed the application on both procedural and substantive grounds.

intake.user_narrative: I am a Police Sergeant attached to the Police Narcotics Bureau. CID officers took me into custody after allegations were made that some PNB officers were involved in drug trafficking, weapons and other serious unlawful activities. I say I was arrested while at work and was not properly told the reason for my arrest. After that, I was detained under the Prevention of Terrorism Act through several detention orders for long periods. My house was searched and items such as pen drives, an external hard drive and SIM cards were taken. I believe my arrest and detention were unfair and affected my police career, liberty and reputation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged unlawful arrest and detention under the PTA and claimed violations of several constitutional rights. The Court held that he failed to establish his version that he was arrested inside the Police Narcotics Bureau premises, particularly because no relevant PNB officers responsible for the premises were made parties. The Court accepted the CID's version that he was summoned to the CID and arrested there. It found sufficient material for reasonable suspicion under the PTA, including a complaint by a PNB officer alleging involvement of PNB officers in drug trafficking and weapons dealings, investigation notes, written authorization, an arrest receipt, items seized from the petitioner's residence, and further investigative material. The Court also held that the detention orders were valid, that non-production before a Magistrate was excused where a detention order was obtained within the PTA time frame, and that the orders signed by the President were not invalid because the President was also the Minister of Defence. Therefore no fundamental rights infringement was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The petition was dismissed with costs. The Court also directed the Inspector General of Police to look into the legality or suitability of allowing the petitioner to continue employment as a police officer, and directed the Attorney General to examine the relevant facts and consider giving necessary advice to the Inspector General of Police.
