retrieved_contexts: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

In SC Application No. 69/88, the petitioner, a clerical employee of the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, challenged her termination through a "vacation of post" notice issued without inquiry. She alleged that she was physically present at work but was denied duties and that the termination was politically motivated following a change in management. She further claimed psychological distress and reputational harm resulting from the abrupt dismissal. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 11 and 14(1)(g). It held that use of disciplinary mechanisms such as "vacation of post" in the absence of factual basis or fair inquiry constituted an abuse of administrative power. The Court found that the termination was arbitrary, lacked procedural fairness, and effectively deprived the petitioner of her lawful occupation. It further held that humiliating removal of an employee without due process amounted to degrading treatment under Article 11. The Court emphasized that public authorities must act as model employers and cannot use administrative discretion to settle personal or political scores. It concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered reinstatement with back wages and costs.

The petitioner, an employee of Robinson Club Bentota Ltd., was suspended following allegations of fraud by management officials. The company operated as a joint venture involving Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation and a foreign corporation. A preliminary objection was raised that the suspension constituted a private employment matter and did not amount to executive or administrative action capable of founding a fundamental rights claim under Article 126. The case involved Article 12(1) concerning equality before the law. The Supreme Court examined the relationship between the State and the corporate entities involved. It held that Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation was effectively a State agency because its shares were held by the Treasury and its directors were state-appointed. The Court further reasoned that the second respondent company functioned as an agent of the State entity, and disciplinary actions carried out through that corporate structure retained the character of executive or administrative action. Distinguishing earlier restrictive decisions concerning statutory corporations, the Court expanded the scope of constitutional jurisdiction where effective state control existed over the entity concerned. Accordingly, the preliminary objection was overruled and the matter was permitted to proceed on its merits within the Supreme Court's fundamental rights jurisdiction.

The Petitioner, a Reserve Sub-Inspector of Police, was suspended from service in 1999 following his arrest on a murder charge. Although he was acquitted in 2011, disciplinary proceedings continued for several years until he was reinstated on August 19, 2016, subject to the condition that he would not receive back wages for the seventeen-year suspension period. The Petitioner challenged the refusal to pay back wages as arbitrary and discriminatory, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed outside the one-month constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2), as the reinstatement letter containing the impugned condition had been issued in August 2016 while the application was filed only in December 2016. The Court upheld the preliminary objection and held that the filing of an administrative appeal did not suspend or renew the constitutional limitation period. The Court further held that reserve police officers were governed by distinct circulars and conditions of service from the regular police force and were entitled to remuneration only for periods during which they actually performed duties. Since the Petitioner had not worked during the suspension period, he possessed no legal entitlement to back wages. The Court also rejected the allegation of discrimination because the Petitioner failed to establish differential treatment compared to similarly situated reservists. The application was accordingly dismissed for being time-barred and lacking substantive merit.

intake.actor_role: municipal council officials and urban development authorities
intake.what_happened: I live in a housing scheme and built a small additional structure in front of my house because of lack of space. The Municipal Commissioner later sent me a letter saying the construction was unauthorized and asking me to remove it. A few days later, municipal officers came to the premises and I say they removed the spiral staircase connected to the structure without first obtaining a court order.
intake.harm_suffered: Threatened demolition of part of the house, alleged removal of access to the upper floor, distress, humiliation, disruption to home life, and fear of losing part of the residence.
intake.user_narrative: I live in a house in the Saranankara Housing Project in Kalubowila. Because my family did not have enough space, I first put up a small temporary structure in front of the house and later made it into a permanent two-storey structure of the same size. The Municipal Commissioner sent me a letter saying the construction was unauthorized and directing me to remove it. Soon after, municipal officers came to the property and I say they removed the spiral staircase without giving me proper notice or first getting a court order. I believe the officials acted unfairly and that my home and family were affected.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that municipal authorities unlawfully required her to demolish an unauthorized structure and removed a spiral staircase, violating Articles 11, 12(1) and 14(1)(h), with leave granted on Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h). The Court held that the Urban Development Authority had validly delegated planning-related powers to local authority officers, including powers connected with enforcement against unauthorized development. The Court also found that the petitioner admitted building a permanent structure without prior approval, that the structure encroached on a common roadway and drain affecting other residents, and that the evidence did not prove that municipal officers removed the spiral staircase or fence. The petitioner therefore failed to establish any infringement of Article 12(1) or 14(1)(h), and the Article 11 allegation was not accepted.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed with no order as to costs. The respondents were directed to demolish the unauthorized construction forthwith in terms of the law and procedure.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation municipal unauthorized-construction case. Useful for false-violation control because the petitioner alleged arbitrary demolition-related action and home interference, but the Court found valid delegated authority, insufficient proof of the alleged removal, and unlawful encroachment by the petitioner onto roadway and drainage space. cases.case_name:
Don Piyasena Karunaratne and Others v. Anuradhapura Municipal Council and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, former occupants of Municipal Council staff quarters, sought transfer of ownership of the houses they had occupied for several decades, relying on a rent-purchase claim and a ministerial direction asserting a long-term expectation of ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal treatment in denial of property transfer. The Respondents argued that the premises were staff quarters not eligible for conversion and that statutory provisions under the housing legislation restricted ownership transfer based on rent thresholds, which the Petitioners exceeded. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were legally ineligible under the governing statutory framework, particularly Section 5(A), which imposed strict eligibility conditions. It further found that the agreements constituted tenancy arrangements rather than enforceable rent-purchase contracts capable of creating ownership rights. The Court also held that no legitimate expectation arose because the Council had made no binding promise but only indicated discretionary future consideration. Accordingly, it concluded that there was no arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application for failure to establish a constitutional violation.

cases.case_name: Ernest Fernando v. Municipal Council of Moratuwa and Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 278/2021, the petitioner challenged the Moratuwa Municipal Council's handling of a housing estate title transfer policy. The Council had introduced a scheme to transfer deeds to long-term occupants at a nominal value, yet the petitioner alleged unequal treatment, claiming that others received deeds while his long-standing occupation was ignored. His claim was complicated by a prior Court of Appeal determination that his purchase agreement was void under the Registration of Title Act. The Supreme Court examined whether there was a violation of Article 12(1) based on alleged unequal application of the policy. The Court found that at the time of filing, no final administrative refusal had been made and the process was still ongoing, rendering the application premature. However, it observed that public authorities must apply policies consistently and fairly, and that long-term possession, including predecessor occupation, could be relevant in assessing entitlement. It emphasized that arbitrary deviation from declared policy may infringe equality guarantees. Despite dismissing the application on procedural grounds, the Court directed the Council to consider the petitioner's eligibility fairly and make a reasoned determination. A dissenting view held that reliance on a void agreement could not establish lawful possession for benefit under the policy.

cases.case_name:
Daya Chandrasiri Jayanetti and Others v. Urban Development Authority (UDA)
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, residents of Chapel Lane, Nugegoda, challenged the operation of Royal Institute and the construction of unauthorized high-rise buildings within a Mixed Development Zone where educational institutions were prohibited under the applicable Development Plan. They alleged that the Urban Development Authority and Kotte Municipal Council unlawfully permitted construction contrary to zoning regulations, including erecting a building with five upper floors on a site below the minimum land extent and situated on a road only six meters wide instead of the required twelve meters. The Petitioners further complained that no Certificate of Conformity had been issued for one building despite occupation by approximately 1,900 students, causing traffic congestion, noise, and restrictions on movement. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h), they argued that the authorities had granted preferential treatment to the school while disregarding the rights of residents. The Court held that the Respondents had violated the Petitioners' fundamental rights by failing to enforce zoning laws and building regulations. It emphasized that occupation without a Certificate of Conformity directly contravened statutory regulations and created serious public safety risks. The Court found the approval of a high-rise building on a narrow road to be an intentional violation of legal requirements and ordered the demolition of the illegal constructions and cancellation of permits within three months.

cases.case_name: Subadra v. Kotikawatte Mulleriyawa Pradeshiya Sabha
cases.summary: The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

cases.case_name: Roberts and Another v. Ratnayake and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners held municipal tenancies and leases for business stalls which were terminated by the Kandy Municipal Council on grounds of unauthorized structural alterations and residential use of commercial premises. They alleged unequal treatment compared to other stallholders who committed similar by-law breaches but were not terminated, invoking Article 12(1) on equality and equal protection. The State contended that termination was lawful due to contractual breaches and municipal by-laws. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were not similarly circumstanced to the other tenants as they had committed both by-law violations and breaches of tenancy agreements. It further held that enforcement of contractual terms does not automatically amount to infringement of fundamental rights unless constitutional arbitrariness is established. The Court found that lawful termination of tenancy under contractual and statutory authority could not be challenged as discriminatory absent proof of identical circumstances and irrational differentiation. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to discharge the burden of proving unequal treatment under Article 12(1), and therefore no fundamental rights violation was established. The application was dismissed.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on freedom of movement and residence. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(h) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

The Petitioners, former occupants of Municipal Council staff quarters, sought transfer of ownership of the houses they had occupied for several decades, relying on a rent-purchase claim and a ministerial direction asserting a long-term expectation of ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal treatment in denial of property transfer. The Respondents argued that the premises were staff quarters not eligible for conversion and that statutory provisions under the housing legislation restricted ownership transfer based on rent thresholds, which the Petitioners exceeded. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were legally ineligible under the governing statutory framework, particularly Section 5(A), which imposed strict eligibility conditions. It further found that the agreements constituted tenancy arrangements rather than enforceable rent-purchase contracts capable of creating ownership rights. The Court also held that no legitimate expectation arose because the Council had made no binding promise but only indicated discretionary future consideration. Accordingly, it concluded that there was no arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application for failure to establish a constitutional violation.

In SC(FR) Application No. 278/2021, the petitioner challenged the Moratuwa Municipal Council's handling of a housing estate title transfer policy. The Council had introduced a scheme to transfer deeds to long-term occupants at a nominal value, yet the petitioner alleged unequal treatment, claiming that others received deeds while his long-standing occupation was ignored. His claim was complicated by a prior Court of Appeal determination that his purchase agreement was void under the Registration of Title Act. The Supreme Court examined whether there was a violation of Article 12(1) based on alleged unequal application of the policy. The Court found that at the time of filing, no final administrative refusal had been made and the process was still ongoing, rendering the application premature. However, it observed that public authorities must apply policies consistently and fairly, and that long-term possession, including predecessor occupation, could be relevant in assessing entitlement. It emphasized that arbitrary deviation from declared policy may infringe equality guarantees. Despite dismissing the application on procedural grounds, the Court directed the Council to consider the petitioner's eligibility fairly and make a reasoned determination. A dissenting view held that reliance on a void agreement could not establish lawful possession for benefit under the policy.

The Court also noted that the petitioners had been warned that the postgraduate business studies they pursued were not relevant for the classification they sought. In addition, the application was filed well outside the one-month period after the revision was communicated, making it time-barred. No infringement of Article 12(1) was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.

intake.incident_location: Kalukele junction on the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road and Aralaganwila Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Aralaganwila Police Station
intake.what_happened: We took part in a village protest at Kalukele junction because wild elephants were repeatedly entering our village and paddy fields, damaging crops and property and causing fear among villagers. The protest blocked the main road for some time. Police later said a Magistrate had issued orders relating to the protest, but those orders were not addressed to us. Several days later, we were summoned to Aralaganwila Police Station, arrested in relation to the protest, produced before the Magistrate and remanded.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, police custody, remand custody for about 14 days, disruption to farming during the Yala cultivation season, alleged loss to paddy fields due to inability to attend to them, distress, restriction of liberty, and fear that the arrest was punishment for joining a protest.
intake.user_narrative: We are villagers from Kalukele. For a long time wild elephants had been entering our village and paddy fields, damaging crops and houses and even causing deaths. Because the authorities had not properly solved the problem, many villagers joined a protest at Kalukele junction to draw attention to our situation. The protest blocked the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road. Police came and later said there were court orders about stopping the protest, but those orders were not addressed to us and we were not personally served with them. We attended a meeting at the police station the next day about the elephant issue. Several days later, we were told to come to the Aralaganwila Police Station, where we were arrested and later remanded. We believe the police unfairly used the criminal process against us for taking part in the protest.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the protest at Kalukele junction, though arising from genuine grievances about the human-elephant conflict, unlawfully blocked the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road and amounted to offences including public nuisance, obstruction and wrongful restraint. Therefore the arrest of the petitioners for being members of an unlawful assembly and causing wrongful restraint was not unlawful, and Article 13(1) was not infringed. The Court also declined to find violations of Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) because of the unlawful character of the protest, and no final relief was granted on the other pleaded Article 14 claims. However, the 1st respondent's B Report did not comply with the law and his request to remand the petitioners was based on arbitrary and insufficient reasons. This caused the petitioners to be detained in remand custody for 14 days, infringing Article 13(2).
gold.gold_remedy: The application was partly allowed. The Court declared that the 1st respondent infringed the petitioners' rights under Article 13(2) and ordered him to pay Rs. 30,000 as compensation from his personal funds to the two petitioners. The Court also directed the Attorney General to convey observations on the human-elephant conflict to relevant executive authorities and file a report within six months, directed the Inspector General of Police to issue a Police Order on protest-related policing principles and file a report within six months, and directed the Registrar to forward copies of the judgment to specified officials.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to form and join trade unions
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Police had previously stated there were court orders relating to stopping the protest, but these orders were not addressed to the villagers and they were not personally served. The arrests occurred several days after the protest.

DIRECT CONSEQUENCES: The villagers were arrested, produced before a Magistrate, and subsequently remanded.

The alleged violation appears to be **(a) A DIRECT act by a state authority acting in official capacity**.

Here's the reasoning:

1.  **The role of the actor involved:** The actors involved are identified as "police officers" from the "Sri Lanka Police, Aralaganwila Police Station." The police are a state institution responsible for law enforcement.
2.  **Whether they were acting in official capacity:** The facts state that the individuals were "summoned to Aralaganwila Police Station, arrested in relation to the protest, produced before the Magistrate and remanded." These actions—summoning, arrest, production before a Magistrate, and remand—are official functions and powers exercised by police officers and the judiciary within the framework of the criminal justice system. They are not actions that can be undertaken by private individuals.
3.  **The relevant constitutional provisions regarding state action:** While the provided constitutional articles do not explicitly define "state action," provisions like Article 13(1) ("No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law") and Article 13(2) ("Every person held in custody... shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court...") describe actions (arrest, detention, production before a judge) that are inherently carried out by state authorities (police, courts) in their official capacity. The alleged violation directly concerns these types of actions.
4.  **Any distinction between personal conduct and official conduct:** The actions described (arrest, production before a Magistrate, remand) are specific powers and duties conferred upon law enforcement and judicial officers by the state. They are clearly distinct from personal conduct and fall squarely within the scope of official duties.

cases.case_name: Bernard Soysa v Attorney-General
cases.summary: On 11 January 1991 the petitioners, who were members of political parties, organized a Satyagraha protest at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa in Kandy to demonstrate against the Gulf War. Police officers intervened, seized posters and placards, and dispersed the gathering. The petitioners maintained that the protest was peaceful and alleged violations of Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution relating to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly. The police contended that the demonstrators were shouting slogans, carrying placards, obstructing access to a sacred religious site, and disturbing public order during a period of civil unrest. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the Maha Maluwa was primarily a place associated with worship and religious observance rather than a public forum intended for political demonstrations. It emphasized that no implied right existed to conduct political protests at such a location without obtaining permission from the relevant religious authorities. The Court further found that the gathering could not be regarded as entirely peaceful because the shouting of slogans and display of placards disrupted the religious atmosphere surrounding the temple premises. Since the freedoms guaranteed under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, the police were entitled to act under existing legal powers to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order at a sensitive religious location.

cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector
Channa Abeyratne and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector Channa Abeyratne and Others arose from a land dispute involving allegations of encroachment by a Buddhist priest. The petitioner claimed that on 7 June 2010 he was forcibly arrested at his residence and detained at Maho Police Station until midnight, during which he was allegedly threatened by the Headquarters Inspector. The respondents denied any arrest, stating that the petitioner voluntarily attended the station upon request to resolve the complaint. Police records indicated the officer-in-charge was away on duty, and an affidavit from the petitioner's uncle confirmed that the petitioner went to the station on his own and left without complaint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 13(1), asserting arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment. The Supreme Court emphasised that in fundamental rights proceedings alleging police misconduct, the burden lies on the petitioner to establish facts with a high degree of probability. It found significant inconsistencies between the petitioner's version and contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence. The Court held that there was no credible proof of arrest within the meaning of law and that the petitioner's attendance at the police station was voluntary. Accordingly, the Court concluded that no infringement of constitutional rights had been established and dismissed the application in its entirety for failure of proof.

cases.case_name:
Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and Others concerned allegations of custodial torture and illegal detention following an arrest on 20 September 2017 by Anuradhapura police officers. The petitioner alleged that he was arrested without explanation, taken to a secluded teak forest near Thisa Wewa, suspended from a tree, and brutally assaulted for two hours before being detained at the police station for four days without medical care or production before a Magistrate. The respondents claimed that he was a drug user who sustained injuries while attempting to flee during questioning related to a stolen motorcycle. Medical evidence, however, confirmed six grievous injuries including a brachial plexus rupture consistent with forceful suspension. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Supreme Court found the respondents' explanation wholly implausible and held that the injuries could only have resulted from deliberate custodial violence. It further held that failure to maintain proper arrest records and failure to produce the petitioner before a Magistrate constituted unlawful detention. The Court concluded that both torture and arbitrary detention were established and held the responsible officers personally liable, awarding compensation and costs from their personal funds.

cases.case_name:
Ven. Aturupalayagama Pragna Surinda Thero and Another v. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station, Minneriya and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

It emphasized that no implied right existed to conduct political protests at such a location without obtaining permission from the relevant religious authorities. The Court further found that the gathering could not be regarded as entirely peaceful because the shouting of slogans and display of placards disrupted the religious atmosphere surrounding the temple premises. Since the freedoms guaranteed under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, the police were entitled to act under existing legal powers to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order at a sensitive religious location.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector
Channa Abeyratne and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector Channa Abeyratne and Others arose from a land dispute involving allegations of encroachment by a Buddhist priest. The petitioner claimed that on 7 June 2010 he was forcibly arrested at his residence and detained at Maho Police Station until midnight, during which he was allegedly threatened by the Headquarters Inspector. The respondents denied any arrest, stating that the petitioner voluntarily attended the station upon request to resolve the complaint. Police records indicated the officer-in-charge was away on duty, and an affidavit from the petitioner's uncle confirmed that the petitioner went to the station on his own and left without complaint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 13(1), asserting arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment. The Supreme Court emphasised that in fundamental rights proceedings alleging police misconduct, the burden lies on the petitioner to establish facts with a high degree of probability. It found significant inconsistencies between the petitioner's version and contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence. The Court held that there was no credible proof of arrest within the meaning of law and that the petitioner's attendance at the police station was voluntary. Accordingly, the Court concluded that no infringement of constitutional rights had been established and dismissed the application in its entirety for failure of proof.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

On 11 January 1991 the petitioners, who were members of political parties, organized a Satyagraha protest at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa in Kandy to demonstrate against the Gulf War. Police officers intervened, seized posters and placards, and dispersed the gathering. The petitioners maintained that the protest was peaceful and alleged violations of Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution relating to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly. The police contended that the demonstrators were shouting slogans, carrying placards, obstructing access to a sacred religious site, and disturbing public order during a period of civil unrest. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the Maha Maluwa was primarily a place associated with worship and religious observance rather than a public forum intended for political demonstrations. It emphasized that no implied right existed to conduct political protests at such a location without obtaining permission from the relevant religious authorities. The Court further found that the gathering could not be regarded as entirely peaceful because the shouting of slogans and display of placards disrupted the religious atmosphere surrounding the temple premises. Since the freedoms guaranteed under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, the police were entitled to act under existing legal powers to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order at a sensitive religious location.

The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector Channa Abeyratne and Others arose from a land dispute involving allegations of encroachment by a Buddhist priest. The petitioner claimed that on 7 June 2010 he was forcibly arrested at his residence and detained at Maho Police Station until midnight, during which he was allegedly threatened by the Headquarters Inspector. The respondents denied any arrest, stating that the petitioner voluntarily attended the station upon request to resolve the complaint. Police records indicated the officer-in-charge was away on duty, and an affidavit from the petitioner's uncle confirmed that the petitioner went to the station on his own and left without complaint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 13(1), asserting arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment. The Supreme Court emphasised that in fundamental rights proceedings alleging police misconduct, the burden lies on the petitioner to establish facts with a high degree of probability. It found significant inconsistencies between the petitioner's version and contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence. The Court held that there was no credible proof of arrest within the meaning of law and that the petitioner's attendance at the police station was voluntary. Accordingly, the Court concluded that no infringement of constitutional rights had been established and dismissed the application in its entirety for failure of proof.

The drama was approved after preview and later scheduled and advertised for telecast. After some delay and after we signed a commercial agreement, the corporation began airing it, but later terminated the telecast before all episodes were shown, saying it was not generating expected ratings and revenue.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of opportunity to fully telecast the teledrama, alleged financial loss after spending personal savings and borrowings on production, loss of commercial opportunity with other channels, disappointment among viewers, and alleged harm to creative and professional work.
intake.user_narrative: We produced a teledrama called La Sanda Pamula after spending our own savings, borrowing money and even mortgaging property. We submitted it to Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation, paid the preview fee, and were told that it had been approved. The corporation later advertised that the drama would be telecast and eventually started airing it after we signed an agreement. However, before all episodes were shown, the corporation sent a notice terminating the telecast. We believe this was unfair because we had invested heavily in the production, the trailer and telecast on Rupavahini affected our ability to offer it to other channels, and viewers were also disappointed by the sudden cancellation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged that Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation unlawfully terminated the telecast of their teledrama and thereby violated constitutional rights including equality, expression, occupation and information-related rights, with leave granted on Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b). The Court held that the dispute arose from a commercial agreement under which the corporation had purchased rights to transmit, retransmit and simulcast the teledrama. The corporation produced viewing ratings and internal reports showing low ratings and insufficient revenue, and the Court accepted that termination was a business decision taken under the agreement. The Court emphasized that every contractual dispute, commercial decision or breach of ordinary rights does not amount to a fundamental rights violation, even where the corporation is amenable to fundamental rights jurisdiction. No fundamental rights violation was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.

cases.case_name: Bennet Rathnayake v Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation
cases.summary: The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Vasudeva Nanayakkara v. Choksy and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners sought enforcement of a prior Supreme Court judgment relating to the annulment of the privatization of the Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation, claiming entitlement to profits earned during a transitional period prior to restoration of state ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) in relation to executive implementation of the earlier judgment. The respondents argued that no profits existed and that the claim was inconsistent with final judicial determinations. The Supreme Court rejected the application, relying on audited financial statements showing that the company had incurred losses during the relevant period. It held that there was no factual or legal basis for claiming interim profits. The Court further emphasized the principle of finality of judgments, stating that court orders cannot be reopened or altered through collateral motions. It held that restitution had already been achieved through restoration of ownership and that no further obligations remained. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation of fundamental rights was found.

cases.case_name:
JPC Trade Company Ltd and R. Lahiru Rakshitha v. Jagath P. Wijeweera and
Others
cases.summary: The 1st Petitioner, a Japanese vehicle exporting company, and its Country Manager were investigated by Sri Lanka Customs on allegations of undervaluing imported vehicles in order to reduce customs duties payable to the State. Investigations disclosed that undervalued pro-forma invoices had been issued to local importers while the remaining balance of the vehicle prices was collected through a local agent and transferred unlawfully to Japan. Following an inquiry conducted under the Customs Ordinance, the 2nd Petitioner was ordered to pay a mitigated forfeiture amounting to Rs. 6,000,000. The Petitioners alleged that their rights under Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(4) had been violated because the importer involved in the transactions had not been similarly punished. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that Article 12 guarantees equality only in the lawful exercise of executive power and does not entitle a party to claim "equal violation of the law." The Court observed that the Petitioners sought to rely upon the alleged failure to prosecute another party in order to avoid lawful consequences arising from their own misconduct. The Court further noted that the Petitioners had deliberately suppressed material facts because the 2nd Petitioner had already admitted involvement in the undervaluation scheme during the Customs investigation despite later claiming otherwise before Court. The Court held that Customs officials were legally bound to act upon the findings of the inquiry under the Customs Ordinance and that the allegations of arbitrary punishment lacked merit. The application was dismissed with costs.

cases.case_name:
Rajaye Thakserukaruwange Sangamaya and Others v. P. P. D. S.
Muthukumarana and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Rajaye Thakserukaruwange Sangamaya and Others v. P. P. D. S. Muthukumarana and Others, a trade union and five government valuers, challenged administrative actions affecting salary increments, seniority deductions, and a revised promotional marking scheme issued in July 2021. They alleged that these measures were retaliatory following trade union activities and discriminated against union members, violating Articles 12(1), 14(1)(d) and 14(1)(g). The State raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed beyond the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2). The Supreme Court examined whether the alleged infringement was continuous and whether a pending Human Rights Commission inquiry could suspend time limits under Section 13(1) of the HRC Act. It held that the publication of the revised marking scheme constituted the last operative act, and therefore the limitation period commenced from that date. The Court further found that the petitioners failed to produce evidence of an ongoing HRC inquiry sufficient to suspend the statutory deadline. Emphasising the mandatory nature of the constitutional time bar, the Court held that bare assertions were insufficient to extend jurisdiction. It concluded that the application was time-barred and dismissed it in limine without examining the substantive merits of the alleged infringement.

cases.case_name: Silva v. Bank of Ceylon
cases.summary: The petitioner challenged the Bank of Ceylon's sale of mortgaged property and its refusal to disclose resale details and remit surplus proceeds after recovery of a loan. The bank had purchased the property at auction and later resold it at a significantly higher price, retaining the excess. The petitioner claimed entitlement to the surplus under statutory and constitutional principles, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The respondents relied on a restrictive interpretation of the Bank of Ceylon Ordinance, arguing no obligation to disclose resale proceeds or pay excess. The Supreme Court held that Section 27 of the Ordinance imposes a statutory duty to return surplus proceeds to the mortgagor after settlement of debt. It further held that refusal to disclose financial details necessary to assert this right was arbitrary and contrary to fairness. The Court emphasized that state-linked financial institutions must act transparently and cannot retain windfall profits beyond lawful entitlement. It found that withholding surplus funds constituted unequal application of law and breach of public trust principles. The petitioner's rights were therefore violated and the bank was directed to disclose, compute, and remit the excess with interest.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Bennet Rathnayake v Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

stage_b_cases.case_name: Silva v. Bank of Ceylon
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner challenged the Bank of Ceylon's sale of mortgaged property and its refusal to disclose resale details and remit surplus proceeds after recovery of a loan. The bank had purchased the property at auction and later resold it at a significantly higher price, retaining the excess. The petitioner claimed entitlement to the surplus under statutory and constitutional principles, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The respondents relied on a restrictive interpretation of the Bank of Ceylon Ordinance, arguing no obligation to disclose resale proceeds or pay excess. The Supreme Court held that Section 27 of the Ordinance imposes a statutory duty to return surplus proceeds to the mortgagor after settlement of debt. It further held that refusal to disclose financial details necessary to assert this right was arbitrary and contrary to fairness. The Court emphasized that state-linked financial institutions must act transparently and cannot retain windfall profits beyond lawful entitlement. It found that withholding surplus funds constituted unequal application of law and breach of public trust principles. The petitioner's rights were therefore violated and the bank was directed to disclose, compute, and remit the excess with interest.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

The petitioner challenged the Bank of Ceylon's sale of mortgaged property and its refusal to disclose resale details and remit surplus proceeds after recovery of a loan. The bank had purchased the property at auction and later resold it at a significantly higher price, retaining the excess. The petitioner claimed entitlement to the surplus under statutory and constitutional principles, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The respondents relied on a restrictive interpretation of the Bank of Ceylon Ordinance, arguing no obligation to disclose resale proceeds or pay excess. The Supreme Court held that Section 27 of the Ordinance imposes a statutory duty to return surplus proceeds to the mortgagor after settlement of debt. It further held that refusal to disclose financial details necessary to assert this right was arbitrary and contrary to fairness. The Court emphasized that state-linked financial institutions must act transparently and cannot retain windfall profits beyond lawful entitlement. It found that withholding surplus funds constituted unequal application of law and breach of public trust principles. The petitioner's rights were therefore violated and the bank was directed to disclose, compute, and remit the excess with interest.

intake.what_happened: I was appointed as a Road Development Officer on a six-month contract basis by the Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority, and the contract was repeatedly extended for several years. After the last contract period ended, I continued reporting to work expecting the usual renewal letter and arrears of salary, but my salary was stopped and I later received a letter saying my services had been terminated with effect from the earlier expiry date.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of employment, non-payment of salary from August 2008, financial hardship, career uncertainty, and alleged retaliatory termination after involvement in a public land and environmental dispute.
intake.user_narrative: I was appointed as a Road Development Officer for the Colombo District on a six-month contract by the Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority. My contract was repeatedly extended for six months at a time, and in the past I would continue working after the expiry date while the formal renewal letter and salary arrears came later. After my last contract period ended, I continued reporting to duty as usual, but my salary was not paid. Later, I received a letter saying my services had been terminated with effect from the earlier expiry date. I believe this was unfair, especially because I had been involved in opposing the use of a state land called Galgoda Kele for a garbage disposal project and had filed a case about that issue.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that termination of his contract appointment as Road Development Officer violated Article 12(1). The Court held that before claiming relief for termination, the petitioner had to establish that his appointment was lawful. The Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority was established by statute, and the power to appoint staff was vested in the Provincial Public Service Commission. The documents relied on by the petitioner showed appointment or extension by the Chairman or General Manager, who had no statutory power to make such appointments. The appointment was therefore devoid of legal effect and null and void, and the Court could not grant relief that would perpetuate an unlawful appointment. Article 12(1) was not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed with no order as to costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation public authority employment termination case. Useful for false-violation control because the petitioner alleged unlawful and retaliatory termination after repeated contract extensions, but the Court rejected the Article 12(1) claim because the underlying appointment itself was legally invalid.
