cases.case_name:
Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG
Rubber Development Dept and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. The Court dismissed the application in limine without examining the substantive merits. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Sathkumara Pathirannehelage Sisira Senanayake v. Land Reform Commission
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner applied for the post of Director Finance at the Land Reform Commission and was selected as the most suitable candidate. By letter dated April 22, 2016, the Commission formally appointed him to the position with effect from May 15, 2016. Acting in reliance on the appointment, the Petitioner resigned from his previous employment. However, on April 28, 2016, the Chairman of the Commission issued a further letter temporarily suspending the appointment without providing any reasons. The Respondents justified the suspension by referring to a Ministry directive ordering an investigation into an appointment. The Petitioner contended that the directive related to the position of Accountant and not to the Director Finance post for which he had been selected. Alleging violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), the Petitioner challenged the legality of the suspension. The Supreme Court held that the Chairman lacked authority to suspend the appointment on the basis of a directive that clearly referred to a different post. The Court further held that suspending a valid appointment without lawful cause, particularly after the Petitioner had resigned from his former employment in reliance upon it, constituted arbitrary and unreasonable executive action. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights to equality and lawful occupation. The suspension letter was declared null and void, and directions were issued requiring the Commission to implement the original appointment within one month.

cases.summary: The Petitioner served as a contract Management Assistant in the Irrigation Department from 2008 and was appointed in November 2014 to the permanent and pensionable post of clerk with effect from October 2014 under Circular No. 25/2014. In August 2015, the Director General of Irrigation cancelled her permanent appointment and subsequently prevented her from reporting for duty. The State contended that the appointment had been issued mistakenly because the relevant circular applied only to employees on salary scale MN1, whereas the Petitioner had been receiving remuneration under the slightly higher MN2 scale. The Petitioner alleged that the cancellation of her permanent appointment violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court held that even if the appointment had resulted from an administrative error, the mistake was attributable to the Government and not to any misconduct by the Petitioner. Applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong, the Court reasoned that the State could not penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials. The Court further held that the issuance of the appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period created a legitimate expectation that the Petitioner would continue in the permanent cadre until retirement. The cancellation of the appointment solely because she earned a slightly higher salary than the minimum threshold was held to be arbitrary and capricious. The Court therefore found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), quashed the cancellation letters, ordered reinstatement with back wages, and awarded compensation against the State.

cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG
Rubber Development Dept and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

step_8.answer:
Here's an analysis of each case:

**Case 1: D.B.D Rajapakshe v. Director General of Irrigation and Others (SC. FR Application No. 418/2015) [2015]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS:**
    *   The Petitioner in this case was initially a contract employee whose services were later made permanent, and then her permanent appointment was cancelled. The user was a contract employee whose contract was repeatedly extended, and then their services were terminated.
    *   The cancellation of the Petitioner's appointment was attributed to an administrative error by the Government, not the Petitioner's fault. The user's termination, after a pattern of extensions and continued work, might also involve an administrative decision or oversight.
    *   The Petitioner had a legitimate expectation of continued employment due to the issuance of a permanent appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period. The user, having had their contract repeatedly extended and continuing to report to duty after the last expiry date, also appears to have had an expectation of renewal.
    *   The termination in *Rajapakshe* was deemed arbitrary and capricious. The user's termination, effective from an earlier expiry date after they had continued working, could similarly be argued as arbitrary.

2.  **COURT DECISION:**
    *   The court found a violation of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g).
    *   The outcome was that the cancellation letters were quashed, the Petitioner was reinstated with back wages, and compensation was awarded against the State.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI:**
    *   The core legal reasoning was that the State cannot penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials, applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong.
    *   The court also held that the issuance of an appointment letter and payment of salary over a period created a legitimate expectation of continued employment until retirement.
    *   The cancellation of an appointment solely due to an administrative error attributable to the State, especially when it affects a legitimate expectation, was considered arbitrary and capricious.

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION:**
    *   This precedent suggests that if the user's termination was due to an administrative decision or error, and the user had a legitimate expectation of continued employment based on the repeated extensions of their contract and the practice of continuing to work after expiry, a court might view the termination as arbitrary and a violation of fundamental rights.
    *   The principle that the State cannot benefit from its own wrong could be relevant if the termination was not a straightforward non-renewal but rather an administrative decision made after the user had continued to perform duties, especially if the termination was backdated.

**Case 2: Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG Rubber Development Dept and Others (S.C. (F.R.) Application No. 109/2015)

retrieved_contexts: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The Petitioner served as a contract Management Assistant in the Irrigation Department from 2008 and was appointed in November 2014 to the permanent and pensionable post of clerk with effect from October 2014 under Circular No. 25/2014. In August 2015, the Director General of Irrigation cancelled her permanent appointment and subsequently prevented her from reporting for duty. The State contended that the appointment had been issued mistakenly because the relevant circular applied only to employees on salary scale MN1, whereas the Petitioner had been receiving remuneration under the slightly higher MN2 scale. The Petitioner alleged that the cancellation of her permanent appointment violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court held that even if the appointment had resulted from an administrative error, the mistake was attributable to the Government and not to any misconduct by the Petitioner. Applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong, the Court reasoned that the State could not penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials. The Court further held that the issuance of the appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period created a legitimate expectation that the Petitioner would continue in the permanent cadre until retirement. The cancellation of the appointment solely because she earned a slightly higher salary than the minimum threshold was held to be arbitrary and capricious. The Court therefore found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), quashed the cancellation letters, ordered reinstatement with back wages, and awarded compensation against the State.

The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. The Court dismissed the application in limine without examining the substantive merits. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Kattankudy Police Station
intake.what_happened: I am a businessman and member of a political party. After I helped report two people who were pretending to be CID officers and allegedly demanding money from a woman to release her husband from police custody, the police later connected me to a complaint that I had assaulted those individuals. I say the police filed a false report, tried to keep me away from election campaign activities, and later arrested me even though I believed only summons had been issued.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, public humiliation, police custody, need to obtain bail, reputational harm, disruption to political campaign activity, and distress from alleged false police action.
intake.user_narrative: I run a business in Kattankudy and I am involved in local political work. A woman I knew called me saying two men claiming to be CID officers had come to her house and demanded money to release her husband, who had been arrested in a cannabis case. I went there with some friends, questioned the two men, realized they were not police officers, and called 119. Later I found out that the police had filed a report saying I had assaulted those men and had disappeared from the area. I believe this report was false and was meant to interfere with my involvement in an upcoming political rally. A few days later, police officers arrested me near the Kattankudy Police Station. I say I was not properly told the reason at the time and that the arrest was politically motivated.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that police falsely implicated and arrested him to hinder his political activities, and claimed violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 12(2), 13(1) and 13(5), with leave granted on Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The Court found significant inconsistencies in the petitioner's version and held that the B Report did not support his claim that the police had sought and been refused an arrest warrant. The Court accepted that there was a complaint alleging assault, that the relevant Penal Code offences were cognizable, and that the police had a lawful basis to arrest without a warrant. It also accepted that the reason for arrest was communicated to the petitioner, including as reflected in his police statement. There was no credible evidence of political discrimination, arbitrary arrest or denial of equal protection.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation police arrest and alleged political discrimination case. Useful for false-violation control because the petitioner's account initially suggested politically motivated arrest, but the Court found the version unsupported and accepted that due process was followed. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of association
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of association. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of association.

We found 3 similar case(s) in our database: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara; H. M. Punchimenike and Another v. D. M. Bandula Saman Dissanayake and

cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

cases.case_name:
H. M. Punchimenike and Another v. D. M. Bandula Saman Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

cases.case_name: Ganeshan Samson Roy v. M.M. Janaka Marasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested and remanded following allegations of financial fraud arising from a complaint by a private individual regarding a disputed transaction involving bank account use and alleged vehicle import fraud. Despite the existence of exculpatory evidence, including recorded communications negating involvement in the alleged scheme, CID officers proceeded with arrest and prosecution. The Petitioner invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2), alleging arbitrary arrest, unequal treatment, and procedural violations. The Supreme Court held that the CID acted mechanically on an unverified complaint without conducting independent assessment of credibility or examining available exculpatory material. It found that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and was therefore arbitrary and unconstitutional. The Court further held that failure to communicate specific grounds of arrest violated constitutional safeguards under Article 13(1). It also imposed liability on the private complainant for instigating wrongful executive action through false allegations. However, it found no violation of Article 13(2) as the requirement of production before a Magistrate was satisfied. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 13(1) had been violated.

cases.case_name: Dodampe Gamage Asantha Aravinda v. Atapattu and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was unlawfully arrested following a dispute and subjected to custodial assault and fabricated drug charges by police officers. He further claimed he was detained without proper legal justification and produced before court on false evidence. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Court found credible evidence supporting allegations of physical assault and fabrication of charges, including inconsistencies in police accounts and lack of lawful justification for arrest. It held that the conduct of police officers amounted to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment under Article 11. The Court further found that failure to inform the Petitioner of reasons for arrest and delay in judicial production violated constitutional safeguards governing personal liberty. It emphasized that Article 13 protections are fundamental checks against abuse of police power. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's rights were violated and ordered compensation, including State liability for the conduct of its officers.

stage_b_cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
stage_b_cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
H. M. Punchimenike and Another v. D. M. Bandula Saman Dissanayake and
Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that the detainee was unlawfully arrested and detained by the TID, denied access and medical care, and subjected to cruel or inhuman treatment, claiming violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2). Leave was granted only under Articles 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2). The Court accepted the respondents' position that the detainee was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act after investigations and intelligence relating to financial transactions allegedly connected to reorganizing the LTTE, that detention orders were obtained under section 9(1) of the PTA, and that there was no credible material showing the detention orders were fabricated, fraudulent or ultra vires. The Court held that the petitioner had not factually or legally supported the challenge to the arrest and detention and that the procedure under the PTA had been followed. No violation of Articles 12(1), 13(1) or 13(2) was established, and the Article 11 allegation was not accepted.

cases.case_name: Veeradas v. Controller of Immigration and Emigration and Others
cases.summary: In SC Application No. 221/88, the petitioner was stopped at an airport boarding gate while attempting to travel abroad to address Amnesty International. An Air Lanka security officer suspected irregularities in the petitioner's passport and detained him, subsequently handing him over to police who produced him before a Magistrate. He was later exonerated when authorities confirmed the passport was genuine. The petitioner alleged that the arrest and detention were politically motivated to prevent him from speaking internationally, violating Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(a), and 14(1)(h). The Supreme Court examined whether the officer's actions were lawful and justified. It held that the arrest was made in good faith based on reasonable suspicion arising from perceived irregularities in the travel document. The Court found statutory protection applicable where a person acts under a bona fide mistake of fact and believes their conduct is justified by law. It further held that the petitioner failed to prove mala fide intent or political suppression. The arrest and detention were therefore not arbitrary or unlawful. The Court concluded that no violation of fundamental rights had occurred and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Kandegedara Priyawansa v. Gotabhaya Rajapakse, Secretary, Ministry of
Defence and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former soldier, was arrested on February 27, 2010, by officers of the Terrorist Investigation Division in connection with the murder investigation of journalist Lasantha Wickramatunga. The arrest was based on information that SIM cards allegedly used by the perpetrators had been purchased using the National Identity Card of one Pitchchai Jesudasan, who claimed that he lost his identity card after consuming liquor with the Petitioner. Following his arrest, the Petitioner was detained under a detention order and later remanded in custody. In August 2013, the Magistrate discharged the Petitioner upon the advice of the Attorney General due to absence of evidence. The Petitioner alleged that he had not been informed of the reasons for his arrest and that the arrest and detention violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that mere suspicion or association with a person who lost an identity card could not amount to reasonable grounds for arrest in relation to a serious offence such as murder. The Court further noted the absence of arrest notes and the failure of the arresting officer to submit an affidavit justifying the arrest. It held that lawful arrest requires objective material supporting reasonable suspicion rather than conjecture or speculation. Since the initial arrest lacked legal foundation, the detention order issued thereafter was also unsupported by sufficient material. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name:
Major Wengappuli Arachchige Samantha v. Inspector Ranjan Samarasinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a Major in the Sri Lanka Army, was arrested following a fatal road traffic accident involving an army vehicle in which a child died and several passengers were injured. Although the Petitioner was a passenger, he was arrested and remanded on suspicion of aiding and abetting the driver. The police justified the arrest on alleged breaches of motor traffic law and concerns of public unrest. The Petitioner invoked Articles 12(1) and 13(1), alleging arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment under law. The Supreme Court held that there was no legal or evidentiary basis for imputing abetment, as mere presence in a vehicle does not constitute participation in a criminal act. It further found that the provisions relied upon by police were misapplied to the facts of the case. The Court rejected the justification of protective custody, holding that arrest cannot be effected for the alleged safety of the person detained. It also found a complete absence of reasonable suspicion, rendering the arrest arbitrary and unconstitutional. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Edward Sivalingam v. Sub Inspector Jayasekera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested on August 4, 2006 at a lodge in Vavuniya while in possession of a National Identity Card, a Methodist Church identification card, and an LTTE travel pass. Following the discovery of a large cache of explosives in a lorry on the previous day, the authorities suspected the Petitioner of involvement in unlawful activities. The Petitioner alleged that officers attached to the Criminal Investigation Department assaulted him with clubs in order to obtain a confession, causing injuries to his arm, head, and back. He was detained for eight months at CID Headquarters and for a further four months at the Boossa Detention Camp pursuant to successive Detention Orders issued under Emergency Regulations. A confession was recorded in Sinhala, and the Petitioner later asserted that he did not understand the language. The Court examined multiple Medico-Legal Reports from doctors in Colombo and Galle, all of which disclosed no injuries or signs of dislocation, thereby contradicting the allegations of torture. The Court further held that the Petitioner's possession of an LTTE travel pass, coupled with the surrounding circumstances relating to the explosives discovery, provided reasonable suspicion justifying arrest and investigation. The Court also found that the Petitioner had deliberately misled the Court regarding his fluency in Sinhala, noting evidence that he had conducted sermons in Sinhala and originated from a Sinhala-speaking area. The detention was held to be lawful under Emergency Regulations, and the Supreme Court concluded that no violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), or 13(2) had been established.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Abeywardena v Inspector General of Police
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner owned and operated "Jackpot Machines" imported under valid licenses and installed in public establishments. In June 1991 the Police seized the machines pursuant to Emergency Regulations introduced by the President prohibiting private jackpot operations. The petitioner challenged the regulations, contending that they discriminated against private operators while exempting lotteries conducted by the State or public corporations. He alleged violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution and argued that the restrictions were unconstitutional despite Article 15(7). The respondents maintained that the regulations were necessary in the interests of public order and national security. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been violated. The Court reasoned that the distinction between private gaming establishments and State lotteries constituted a valid classification because private jackpot centers had been associated with narcotics, prostitution, and terrorism. It held that Article 12 does not require perfect legislative symmetry and that the State may selectively eliminate perceived threats to public order. The Court further observed that Article 14(1)(g) protects only lawful occupations, and once the regulations rendered jackpot operations unlawful, constitutional protection ceased. The President's subjective satisfaction regarding the necessity of Emergency Regulations could not be reviewed absent proof of mala fides. The Court also emphasized that equitable relief requires clean hands and cannot legitimize illegal conduct.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

The petitioner owned and operated "Jackpot Machines" imported under valid licenses and installed in public establishments. In June 1991 the Police seized the machines pursuant to Emergency Regulations introduced by the President prohibiting private jackpot operations. The petitioner challenged the regulations, contending that they discriminated against private operators while exempting lotteries conducted by the State or public corporations. He alleged violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution and argued that the restrictions were unconstitutional despite Article 15(7). The respondents maintained that the regulations were necessary in the interests of public order and national security. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been violated. The Court reasoned that the distinction between private gaming establishments and State lotteries constituted a valid classification because private jackpot centers had been associated with narcotics, prostitution, and terrorism. It held that Article 12 does not require perfect legislative symmetry and that the State may selectively eliminate perceived threats to public order. The Court further observed that Article 14(1)(g) protects only lawful occupations, and once the regulations rendered jackpot operations unlawful, constitutional protection ceased. The President's subjective satisfaction regarding the necessity of Emergency Regulations could not be reviewed absent proof of mala fides. The Court also emphasized that equitable relief requires clean hands and cannot legitimize illegal conduct.

The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

In SC Application No. 221/88, the petitioner was stopped at an airport boarding gate while attempting to travel abroad to address Amnesty International. An Air Lanka security officer suspected irregularities in the petitioner's passport and detained him, subsequently handing him over to police who produced him before a Magistrate. He was later exonerated when authorities confirmed the passport was genuine. The petitioner alleged that the arrest and detention were politically motivated to prevent him from speaking internationally, violating Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(a), and 14(1)(h). The Supreme Court examined whether the officer's actions were lawful and justified. It held that the arrest was made in good faith based on reasonable suspicion arising from perceived irregularities in the travel document. The Court found statutory protection applicable where a person acts under a bona fide mistake of fact and believes their conduct is justified by law. It further held that the petitioner failed to prove mala fide intent or political suppression. The arrest and detention were therefore not arbitrary or unlawful. The Court concluded that no violation of fundamental rights had occurred and dismissed the application.

intake.incident_location: Ceylon Petroleum Corporation, Colombo 9
intake.actor_name: Ceylon Petroleum Corporation
intake.actor_role: public corporation officials and human resources authorities
intake.what_happened: I am an employee of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and applied for internal promotion to the post of Officer (Audit) Grade A7. After applications were called, the marking scheme used at the interview was different from the marking scheme in the notice. I was not selected, while several other employees were promoted. I believe I should have received marks for my Chartered Accountancy Executive Level qualification and that the change in the marking scheme unfairly affected my chance of promotion.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of promotion opportunity, career progression delay, alleged unfair selection process, lower marks for qualifications, and disadvantage compared with selected candidates.
intake.user_narrative: I have worked at the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation for many years, first as an Accounts Clerk and later in audit-related roles. When applications were called for the Officer (Audit) Grade A7 post, I applied because I believed I had the required qualifications. I later found out that the marking scheme used at the interview was different from the one stated when applications were called. I also believe my Chartered Accountancy Executive Level qualification should have been treated as equivalent to a diploma and given more marks. Several others were selected while I was not. I feel the process was unfair and that I lost a promotion I should have received.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner challenged her non-selection for promotion to Officer (Audit) Grade A7, arguing that the marking scheme was changed after applications were called and that she was denied marks for an ICASL Executive Level qualification. The Court accepted that changing a marking scheme without informing applicants can create a prima facie equality issue and that transparency is required in promotion processes. However, the Court found that the change to the marking scheme was introduced in good faith as part of a broader restructuring, that the petitioner benefited from the increased marks for seniority, and that the decisive issue was whether she possessed the relevant ICASL certificate at the required time. Although she had completed the components, she was certified only after applications closed and after the interview. Therefore, even if the original marking scheme had applied, she was not entitled to the additional marks, no prejudice was caused, and Article 12(1) was not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation public corporation promotion case with an initially plausible procedural fairness issue. Useful for false-violation and weak-article control because the Court recognized a prima facie concern about changing promotion criteria, but rejected the Article 12(1) claim after finding no prejudice and no entitlement to the claimed qualification marks. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of association
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of association. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(c) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or national economy.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
