cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: Hewa Kulasuriyage Anura Nimal v. Commissioner General of Excise
cases.summary: The petitioner, an excise inspector, challenged a promotion decision alleging incorrect allocation of marks for seniority and merit, resulting in exclusion from the final list. The respondents contended that the selection process followed the established Scheme of Recruitment and that marks were awarded consistently across all candidates. The Supreme Court held that promotion assessments fall within the lawful administrative discretion of relevant authorities, particularly where structured evaluation criteria exist. It found no evidence of mala fides, bias, or deviation from prescribed marking procedures. The Court further held that dissatisfaction with scoring outcomes alone does not constitute a constitutional violation unless supported by proof of arbitrariness or unequal application of rules. It concluded that the petitioner was evaluated under the same framework as other candidates and that no differential or discriminatory treatment occurred. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, affirming that equality under Article 12(1) requires demonstrable departure from legal standards rather than subjective disagreement with administrative scoring.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

cases.case_name:
W.K.B. Seneviratne and 5 Others v. Justice P.R.P. Perera, Chairman, Public
Service Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Class II Jailors in the Department of Prisons, challenged the promotion of the 15th to 23rd Respondents to the rank of Class I Jailors. The promotions were conducted under a 2004 marking scheme allocating marks for seniority, experience, performance, and presentation at an interview. The Petitioners alleged that the promotions violated Article 12(1) because several selected officers were junior to them in service and because the marking scheme introduced subjectivity. They also contended that an inquiry was pending against the 17th Respondent, making that promotion improper. The Respondents maintained that the governing recruitment scheme lawfully permitted promotions based on both seniority and merit. The Court held that seniority alone was not the exclusive criterion in public service promotions and that the applicable recruitment framework authorized the consideration of efficiency and performance. Although the Court acknowledged that interview presentation marks introduced some degree of subjectivity, it found this acceptable because such marks represented only a limited portion of the total evaluation and were assessed by a balanced panel. The Court further determined that the Petitioners had failed to provide any specific evidence regarding the alleged inquiry against the 17th Respondent. The Supreme Court concluded that the marking scheme constituted an objective method of appraisal ensuring fairness among eligible candidates and held that the Petitioners failed to establish any infringement of the right to equality and equal protection of the law.

cases.case_name:
Weerathunga Arachchige Michael Padmasiri and Others v. The Governor –
Southern Province and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, officers of the Co-operative Development Department, challenged revised Schemes of Recruitment introduced in 2015 and implemented through 2016 selection processes, which introduced new marking criteria based on higher educational qualifications and professional training. They alleged that the new criteria were arbitrary and disadvantaged existing officers, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Supreme Court dismissed the application on the preliminary ground of limitation under Article 126(2). It held that the Petitioners had knowledge of the impugned scheme once official vacancy notices were published in March 2016 and participated in the selection process without objection. The Court found that such participation constituted acquiescence, preventing them from later challenging the legality of the process after failing to secure selection. It further held that the application was filed beyond the mandatory one-month period and therefore was jurisdictionally barred. The Court did not proceed to examine the substantive fairness of the recruitment criteria. Accordingly, the application was dismissed as time-barred without a finding on the merits.

retrieved_contexts: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

The petitioner, an excise inspector, challenged a promotion decision alleging incorrect allocation of marks for seniority and merit, resulting in exclusion from the final list. The respondents contended that the selection process followed the established Scheme of Recruitment and that marks were awarded consistently across all candidates. The Supreme Court held that promotion assessments fall within the lawful administrative discretion of relevant authorities, particularly where structured evaluation criteria exist. It found no evidence of mala fides, bias, or deviation from prescribed marking procedures. The Court further held that dissatisfaction with scoring outcomes alone does not constitute a constitutional violation unless supported by proof of arbitrariness or unequal application of rules. It concluded that the petitioner was evaluated under the same framework as other candidates and that no differential or discriminatory treatment occurred. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, affirming that equality under Article 12(1) requires demonstrable departure from legal standards rather than subjective disagreement with administrative scoring.

The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

intake.harm_suffered: Fear of landslide or rockslide, risk to house and family safety, anxiety from nearby construction, alleged failure to properly investigate complaints, and concern that public construction was approved despite safety objections.
intake.user_narrative: I own a property in Galle. A nearby lot in the original plan had been reserved for a common well, but the well was later abandoned and filled. Authorities then started building a two-storey community hall on that lot. I was already worried because the land near my house has a slope with rocks and drainage problems, and I had complained before about water and soil movement from the neighbouring property. When I saw excavation and construction starting, I complained to the police, the Municipal Council, the Divisional Secretary, the Urban Development Authority and the National Building Research Organization because I feared the construction would make the land unstable and endanger my family and property. I believe the authorities ignored my safety concerns and allowed the building to continue unfairly.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that construction of a community hall on Lot 9, previously reserved for a common well, violated Article 12(1) because it was unsafe, contrary to Urban Development Authority regulations, inconsistent with National Building Research Organization recommendations, and inadequately investigated. The Court rejected the time-bar objection because the construction and complaints could be treated as a continuing issue. On the merits, the Court held that the authorities could relax the relevant site extent and width requirements under Regulation 17(3), and that the construction was not outlawed. The Court also found that the NBRO recommendations relied on by the petitioner concerned the eastern boundary between the petitioner's property and the 9th respondent's land, not the community hall site, and that NBRO material relating to the community hall did not show danger. There was no material establishing arbitrary, discriminatory or unequal treatment, so Article 12(1) was not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.

cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: M.J.M. Faril et al v. Bandaragama Pradeshiya Sabha et al.
cases.summary: The Petitioners, representing the Wekada Jumma Mosque, obtained approval to construct a two-storey school building and completed the ground floor. During construction of the upper floor, authorities observed deviations from the approved plan, including installation of a concrete slab rather than the approved roof structure. Local residents and Buddhist monks protested, alleging the building was being converted into a mosque. Under community pressure, the Petitioners signed an undertaking affirming the premises would be used solely as a school, after which amended plans were approved. Subsequently, police ordered suspension of construction to prevent an anticipated breach of peace arising from escalating communal tension and continued allegations of religious use. The Petitioners alleged violations of Articles 10, 12(1), and 14(1)(e), claiming interference with religious freedom and discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court held that the authorities acted lawfully to preserve public order and communal harmony. It found that evidence indicated non-compliance with the original permit and failure to obtain mandatory approval required for construction connected to religious education under applicable circulars. The Court further held that the suspension was motivated by legitimate public order concerns rather than religious or racial discrimination. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to establish arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Dharmarathne and Others v. Divisional Secretary, Udapalatha
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged prolonged administrative confusion regarding the territorial boundaries and jurisdictional authority of their village, resulting in repeated referrals between local authorities without final resolution. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal and inconsistent administrative treatment. The respondents contended that the issue arose from technical boundary ambiguities requiring determination by competent delimitation authorities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the hardship faced by the petitioners but held that the matter constituted an administrative boundary dispute rather than a deliberate infringement of fundamental rights. It found no evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal treatment targeted at the petitioners. However, the Court observed systemic delays and lack of coordination between relevant authorities. It directed the Divisional Secretary and Surveyor General to take steps to expedite submission of recommendations to the National Delimitation Commission for resolution of the boundary issue. The Court concluded that while no fundamental rights violation was established, the petitioners were entitled to administrative resolution of their grievance.

cases.case_name: Subadra v. Kotikawatte Mulleriyawa Pradeshiya Sabha
cases.summary: The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

cases.case_name: Siriwardena and Others v. Brigadier J. Rodrigo and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners held minor leases over a land known as "Gallewatta," which had originally vested in the Land Reform Commission before being transferred to the State. Following the transfer, the first and second respondents, acting under the Land Grant (Special Provisions) Law, sought to redistribute the land in small allotments. The petitioners alleged that they were being unfairly evicted and discriminated against in comparison to leaseholders of two nearby lands that remained vested in the Land Reform Commission. They further alleged that the respondents acted under political pressure exerted by a Member of Parliament. The petitioners relied on Articles 12(1) and 12(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established. The Court reasoned that once "Gallewatta" became State land, it entered a distinct legal category different from lands that remained under the Land Reform Commission, and therefore the petitioners were not similarly situated to the other leaseholders. The Court further held that any alleged discrimination arose at the stage when the land was originally vested in the State, but the petitioners had failed to challenge that order within the prescribed time. The Court also found no evidence that the officials had acted under political influence and concluded that they had exercised their functions independently.

retrieved_contexts: Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.
Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(b) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Restrictions on freedom of movement and residence. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(h) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

I was later transferred and had to report to Colombo while pregnant. I requested a transfer closer to Galle or Elpitiya on health grounds because of long travel and pregnancy, but the transfer order was delayed while an inquiry was pending against me based on a complaint by the same officer.
intake.harm_suffered: Workplace distress, alleged sexual harassment, disciplinary black mark, delayed transfer, long-distance travel while pregnant, miscarriage, mental trauma, and alleged obstruction of police service duties and career rights.
intake.user_narrative: I am a woman Sub-Inspector in the Sri Lanka Police attached to the Terrorism Investigation Division. While I was working at the Boosa unit, a senior officer repeatedly made inappropriate advances and remarks to me, which I rejected. I complained about his behaviour, but I feel my complaint was not properly acted on. Instead, there was an inquiry against me after he complained that I had insulted him. I was later required to report to Colombo even though I was pregnant and had to travel a very long distance from the Galle area. I requested a transfer closer to home on health grounds because I was advised to avoid long travel and strenuous activity. The transfer was eventually given, but only after a delay, and I suffered a miscarriage. I believe the authorities treated me unfairly and failed to protect me as a pregnant female police officer.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged sexual harassment, discriminatory treatment as a female police officer, disciplinary unfairness and delay in granting a pregnancy-related transfer. Leave to proceed was granted only under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) in respect of the transfer. The Court held that the petitioner had not provided sufficient evidence to establish a link between the alleged remarks or harassment and the transfer decision, and that it was not required to examine the alleged failure to hold an inquiry against the 1st respondent. The requested transfer was approved within about two months and six days, and the respondents explained the delay by reference to the pending disciplinary inquiry and the petitioner's leave-related absence. The Court was also not convinced by the medical letters relied on by the petitioner and found no substantial connection between the alleged delay and her pregnancy or miscarriage. No violation of Articles 12(1) or 14(1)(g) was established, and the gender discrimination allegation under Article 12(2) was not accepted.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.

The alleged failure to protect the officer and the delayed transfer, especially given her pregnancy, are actions (or inactions) by the police administration.

Therefore, the alleged violation appears to stem from direct executive or administrative actions by state authorities.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

cases.case_name: L. Saman Kumara v. U. L. Perera and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a District Medical Officer attached to the District Hospital in Kandana, was summarily transferred to the Medical Support Division in Colombo following an incident in which he was allegedly obstructed by a group. The transfer was described as being necessitated by service exigencies, and approval from the Public Service Commission was sought retrospectively. As the petitioner was not formally released from his previous station, he remained without salary for nearly four months. The petitioner alleged that the transfer process and related administrative actions violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the authorities failed to provide adequate details regarding the alleged service exigencies or accusations against the petitioner, thereby preventing him from effectively exercising his right to appeal to the Public Service Commission. The Court further held that the failure to comply with Rule 224 of the Public Service Commission Rules directly caused the non-payment of salary and imposed unnecessary hardship upon the petitioner. Although the Ministry may have possessed concerns regarding the petitioner's conduct, the Court concluded that transferring a public officer without transparency, procedural compliance, or an opportunity to respond constituted arbitrary administrative action inconsistent with equality and equal protection of the law. Compensation and costs were awarded against the responsible respondents and the State.

cases.case_name: K.P.K.L.P. Maduwanthi v. S.M.G.K. Perera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a senior officer of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged her transfer to the Ministry pool after an earlier approved transfer to Dambulla was deferred due to allegations of conflict of interest involving her husband's alleged acquisition of state land through irregular transactions. She alleged violation of Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g), claiming arbitrariness and infringement of legitimate expectation. The Supreme Court held that the transfer was justified under Public Service Commission rules permitting reassignment during investigations into misconduct. It found that the Petitioner had made material misrepresentations regarding her husband's business interests, thereby attracting the clean hands doctrine and disentitling her from relief in equity. The Court further held that placement in the pool was necessary to prevent interference with ongoing investigations and to ensure administrative integrity. It also concluded that no legitimate expectation can arise where the expected outcome would facilitate a conflict of interest or improper conduct. Additionally, the Court directed referral of the matter for corruption investigation. Accordingly, it held that there was no violation of fundamental rights and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
S.D.P.W. Waidyarathne v. Provincial Commissioner Local Government, NWP
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, an Ayurvedic medical officer attached to the Mawathagama Pradeshiya Sabha, challenged her transfer to the Bingiriya Pradeshiya Sabha effected in March 2011. She alleged that the transfer was arbitrary, unlawful, and motivated by retaliation arising from complaints she had previously made to the Human Rights Commission and from discrimination connected to her spinal injury. The Respondents maintained that the transfer was necessitated by administrative exigencies and referred to an investigative report indicating that the Petitioner had created workplace conflict, including an incident involving the burning of photocopies of official documents and cheques, thereby causing disharmony with superiors and colleagues. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), the Petitioner contended that the transfer unlawfully interfered with her equality and occupational rights. The Court dismissed the application and held that the transfer was a valid administrative measure justified by exigencies of service. It reasoned that the efficient functioning of a public institution required cooperative relationships between officers and management and that transferring an officer who was in serious conflict with superiors could legitimately restore administrative harmony. The Court further observed that although employers may sympathetically consider medical conditions, an employee cannot insist on serving at a specific workplace as a legal entitlement, particularly where no medical evidence had been presented before the transfer decision. The Court additionally held that the authority to transfer Ayurvedic medical officers had been lawfully delegated and noted that the Petition improperly challenged only the notification communicating the appeal outcome rather than the original transfer order itself.

cases.case_name: Wijesooriya v. Abeyrathne
cases.summary: The petitioner, a police sub-inspector, was transferred from one station to another and alleged that the transfer was not routine administrative action but a punitive measure motivated by personal and political bias due to his involvement in investigations against political associates of a superior officer. The case concerned Article 12(1) of the Constitution on equality and equal protection of the law, alongside arguments relating to occupational rights. The Supreme Court examined whether the transfer constituted bona fide administrative action or an abuse of discretionary power. It held that while the State possesses authority to transfer officers for administrative efficiency, such power must be exercised for legitimate purposes and not as disguised punishment. The Court found that the petitioner was singled out without adherence to proper disciplinary or procedural safeguards, indicating arbitrariness and mala fide intent. It further held that equality under Article 12(1) requires public officers to be treated according to established rules and not subjected to selective adverse treatment. The transfer was found to be an abuse of power and a violation of constitutional guarantees of equality. Accordingly, the Court quashed the transfer order and granted relief including compensation and costs.

cases.case_name: Lakmali v. Gunarathne and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a pregnant woman, alleged that police officers assaulted her at Imaduwa Police Station while she was inquiring about her detained husband. She claimed she was kicked in the abdomen, arrested, and detained overnight, after which she suffered a miscarriage supported by medical evidence linking it to trauma. She alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The respondents denied wrongdoing, but the Supreme Court found the medical and clinical evidence conclusively established causation between the assault and miscarriage. It held that the use of force against a pregnant woman was grossly disproportionate, unlawful, and shocking to conscience. The Court further held that custodial violence of this nature violates the most basic principles of human dignity and equality before the law. It emphasized that police officers acting with malice outside lawful authority are personally liable for their actions. The Court found that the arrest and detention were arbitrary and unjustified, and concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated. Compensation was awarded against individual officers and partially against the State.

Here is an analysis of each case:

**Case 1: Wijesooriya v. Abeyrathne [2001]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS:**
    *   Both the petitioner in the current situation and the petitioner in Wijesooriya v. Abeyrathne are police sub-inspectors.
    *   Both situations involve a transfer of a police officer.
    *   In both instances, it is alleged that the transfer was not a routine administrative action but rather a punitive measure or motivated by improper reasons (personal and political bias in Wijesooriya; alleged retaliation for rejecting advances and reporting a senior officer, and a delayed transfer while pregnant in the current situation).
    *   The Wijesooriya case involved the petitioner being singled out without adherence to proper disciplinary or procedural safeguards, which appears similar to the current petitioner's experience of an inquiry against her after she complained about a senior officer, and a delayed transfer.

2.  **COURT DECISION:**
    *   The court found a violation of fundamental rights, specifically Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The transfer order was quashed, and relief including compensation and costs was granted.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI:**
    *   The core legal reasoning was that while the State has the authority to transfer officers for administrative efficiency, this power must be exercised for legitimate purposes and not as a disguised punishment. The court held that such power must not be arbitrary or mala fide. Equality under Article 12(1) requires public officers to be treated according to established rules and not subjected to selective adverse treatment without proper disciplinary or procedural safeguards.

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION:**
    *   Based on this case, a court might view the current situation critically if the delayed transfer and the inquiry against the petitioner are perceived as punitive measures or motivated by improper reasons (e.g., retaliation for rejecting advances and complaining), rather than legitimate administrative actions. The precedent suggests that if the administrative actions, such as the delayed transfer or the inquiry, were not conducted according to established rules, lacked proper procedural safeguards, or were arbitrary or mala fide, they could be considered a violation of the petitioner's fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1).

**Case 2: L. Saman Kumara v. U. L. Perera and Others [2017]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS:**
    *   Both situations involve a public officer (a District Medical Officer in Saman Kumara, a Sub-Inspector in the current situation) who was transferred.
    *   In both cases, there are allegations of procedural irregularities or arbitrary administrative actions related to the transfer process. The current petitioner alleges her complaint was not properly acted on, and her transfer was delayed while an inquiry was pending against her, similar to the lack of transparency and procedural compliance alleged in Saman Kumara.
    *   Both petitioners suffered hardship as a result of the administrative actions (without salary for nearly four months in Saman Kumara; long-distance travel while pregnant, delayed transfer, and miscarriage in the current situation).

2.  **COURT DECISION:**
    *   The court found a violation of fundamental rights, specifically Article 12(1). Compensation and costs were awarded against the responsible respondents and the State.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI:**
    *   The core legal reasoning was that transferring a public officer without transparency, procedural compliance (such as failing to provide adequate details regarding service exigencies or accusations, thereby preventing an effective appeal, or non-compliance with specific rules), or an opportunity to respond constitutes arbitrary administrative action. Such arbitrary action was deemed inconsistent with equality and equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION:**
    *   Based on this case, a court might view the current situation as a potential violation of Article 12(1) if the delayed transfer, especially given the petitioner's pregnancy and health grounds, and the inquiry against her were carried out without transparency, proper procedural compliance, or an adequate opportunity for her to respond. The precedent suggests that if the authorities failed to act on her complaint properly or delayed her transfer arbitrarily, causing her hardship, such actions could be considered inconsistent with equality and equal protection of the law.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

The petitioner, a police sub-inspector, was transferred from one station to another and alleged that the transfer was not routine administrative action but a punitive measure motivated by personal and political bias due to his involvement in investigations against political associates of a superior officer. The case concerned Article 12(1) of the Constitution on equality and equal protection of the law, alongside arguments relating to occupational rights. The Supreme Court examined whether the transfer constituted bona fide administrative action or an abuse of discretionary power. It held that while the State possesses authority to transfer officers for administrative efficiency, such power must be exercised for legitimate purposes and not as disguised punishment. The Court found that the petitioner was singled out without adherence to proper disciplinary or procedural safeguards, indicating arbitrariness and mala fide intent. It further held that equality under Article 12(1) requires public officers to be treated according to established rules and not subjected to selective adverse treatment. The transfer was found to be an abuse of power and a violation of constitutional guarantees of equality. Accordingly, the Court quashed the transfer order and granted relief including compensation and costs.

The petitioner, a District Medical Officer attached to the District Hospital in Kandana, was summarily transferred to the Medical Support Division in Colombo following an incident in which he was allegedly obstructed by a group. The transfer was described as being necessitated by service exigencies, and approval from the Public Service Commission was sought retrospectively. As the petitioner was not formally released from his previous station, he remained without salary for nearly four months. The petitioner alleged that the transfer process and related administrative actions violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the authorities failed to provide adequate details regarding the alleged service exigencies or accusations against the petitioner, thereby preventing him from effectively exercising his right to appeal to the Public Service Commission. The Court further held that the failure to comply with Rule 224 of the Public Service Commission Rules directly caused the non-payment of salary and imposed unnecessary hardship upon the petitioner. Although the Ministry may have possessed concerns regarding the petitioner's conduct, the Court concluded that transferring a public officer without transparency, procedural compliance, or an opportunity to respond constituted arbitrary administrative action inconsistent with equality and equal protection of the law. Compensation and costs were awarded against the responsible respondents and the State.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that officials unlawfully entered the property and demolished a boundary parapet wall while he was pursuing administrative relief regarding divestment of part of acquired land. The Court held that the relevant portion of land had been acquired by the State under an order made under proviso (a) to section 38 of the Land Acquisition Act, and that under section 40A(a) the order was conclusive evidence of State title so long as it was not revoked. The petitioner had handed over vacant possession, and the Urban Development Authority had already informed him by letter to demolish the parapet wall because it obstructed road development work. Since the wall was on land acquired by and possessed by the State, and the demolition occurred more than one month after notice, no unlawful act or Article 12(1) violation was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.

cases.case_name: Dharmarathne and Others v. Divisional Secretary, Udapalatha
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged prolonged administrative confusion regarding the territorial boundaries and jurisdictional authority of their village, resulting in repeated referrals between local authorities without final resolution. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal and inconsistent administrative treatment. The respondents contended that the issue arose from technical boundary ambiguities requiring determination by competent delimitation authorities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the hardship faced by the petitioners but held that the matter constituted an administrative boundary dispute rather than a deliberate infringement of fundamental rights. It found no evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal treatment targeted at the petitioners. However, the Court observed systemic delays and lack of coordination between relevant authorities. It directed the Divisional Secretary and Surveyor General to take steps to expedite submission of recommendations to the National Delimitation Commission for resolution of the boundary issue. The Court concluded that while no fundamental rights violation was established, the petitioners were entitled to administrative resolution of their grievance.

cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Subadra v. Kotikawatte Mulleriyawa Pradeshiya Sabha
cases.summary: The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

cases.case_name:
D. Wathsala Subhashini De Silva and Another v. Hasitha Kesara Wettimuni and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioners challenged the denial of school admission under a proximity-based quota system, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The authorities rejected admission to Grade 1 at a national school despite ownership of the residential premises and supporting utility documentation. The dispute centered on whether authorities could distinguish between two houses within the same family compound for proximity calculation purposes. The respondents argued that the application was based on incorrect residency representation and that the relevant assessment should be made from the actual occupied house used for residence. The Supreme Court held that where a family owns an entire property compound and no competing occupancy exists, school authorities cannot arbitrarily distinguish between buildings within the same premises for admission assessment. It found that the rejection was based on an unjustified investigative approach that treated internal residential arrangement as determinative. The Court emphasized that documentary evidence already supported the petitioners' residence claim and that authorities had no basis to override ownership and occupancy facts. It concluded that the denial of admission was arbitrary and amounted to unequal treatment under Article 12(1). The Court declared a violation and ordered immediate admission of the child.

cases.case_name:
Maligawa Tours and Exports (PVT) Ltd. v. The Land Reform Commission and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner company challenged a directive issued by the Land Reform Commission seeking recovery of two land parcels long possessed under transfers dating back several decades, including properties used for plantation and tourism purposes. The Commission sought to invalidate prior transfers without prior hearing, despite decades of administrative inaction. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1), asserting arbitrary state interference and breach of legitimate expectation. The Supreme Court held that although no immediate deprivation had occurred, the threatened action constituted an imminent infringement of constitutional rights. It found that the Commission's attempt to reverse long-settled property arrangements without invoking proper statutory procedures was arbitrary and inconsistent with principles of legality. The Court further held that failure to afford a hearing violated natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. It emphasised that administrative silence over prolonged periods cannot be abruptly reversed without lawful justification. The Court also rejected reliance on public pressure as a basis for administrative action. Accordingly, it declared that the proposed takeover would violate Article 12(1) if implemented and granted relief preventing the unlawful interference.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Subadra v. Kotikawatte Mulleriyawa Pradeshiya Sabha
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Dharmarathne and Others v. Divisional Secretary, Udapalatha
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners challenged prolonged administrative confusion regarding the territorial boundaries and jurisdictional authority of their village, resulting in repeated referrals between local authorities without final resolution. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal and inconsistent administrative treatment. The respondents contended that the issue arose from technical boundary ambiguities requiring determination by competent delimitation authorities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the hardship faced by the petitioners but held that the matter constituted an administrative boundary dispute rather than a deliberate infringement of fundamental rights. It found no evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal treatment targeted at the petitioners. However, the Court observed systemic delays and lack of coordination between relevant authorities. It directed the Divisional Secretary and Surveyor General to take steps to expedite submission of recommendations to the National Delimitation Commission for resolution of the boundary issue. The Court concluded that while no fundamental rights violation was established, the petitioners were entitled to administrative resolution of their grievance.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

retrieved_contexts: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(b) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony.
Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Restrictions on freedom of movement and residence. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(h) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

The petitioners challenged prolonged administrative confusion regarding the territorial boundaries and jurisdictional authority of their village, resulting in repeated referrals between local authorities without final resolution. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal and inconsistent administrative treatment. The respondents contended that the issue arose from technical boundary ambiguities requiring determination by competent delimitation authorities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the hardship faced by the petitioners but held that the matter constituted an administrative boundary dispute rather than a deliberate infringement of fundamental rights. It found no evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal treatment targeted at the petitioners. However, the Court observed systemic delays and lack of coordination between relevant authorities. It directed the Divisional Secretary and Surveyor General to take steps to expedite submission of recommendations to the National Delimitation Commission for resolution of the boundary issue. The Court concluded that while no fundamental rights violation was established, the petitioners were entitled to administrative resolution of their grievance.

The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

The Court also noted that after the search the officers secured the house with new locks, kept the keys safely, placed a guard and informed the Grama Niladhari. The Court found no malice, arbitrariness or discrimination and held that Article 12(1) was not infringed; the other alleged articles were not accepted.
